articles.title: Anthropic's Elvis lawsuit shows why AI companies need to face the music
articles.content: Elvis Presley has been dead for nearly 50 years, but apparently even the 'King of Rock and Roll' can't escape the AI industry's appetite for training data. The owners of 274 Elvis songs made famous by Presley have sued Anthropic , accusing the company behind Claude of using his music without permission to build its AI models, and are seeking tens of millions of dollars in damages. AI companies should have to take copyright seriously too, even if that makes their business models more expensive. Anthropic disputes the allegations and says it intends to defend the case. AI companies have long argued that training models on copyrighted works can qualify as fair use, an issue courts are still working through. There's an important legal difference between learning patterns from existing material and reproducing protected expression, but that distinction has become a remarkably convenient place for the AI industry to hide its enormous dependence on other people's creativity. It's hard to sympathize with the companies on the receiving end of these sorts of lawsuits, even when the plaintiffs are not without resources of their own. Unfortunately, these disputes are becoming all too normal. AI-powered music is becoming more widespread , if not necessarily popular , and we've reached a point where discovering that an AI company allegedly used hundreds of copyrighted songs without permission barely qualifies as surprising news. The only unusual part is that this time the person whose music is at the center of the dispute happens to be Elvis Presley. A little less uncompensated song use The lawsuit makes an accusation that goes beyond simply using copyrighted material for training. According to the complaint, Claude could generate material that closely resembled existing Elvis songs, even after Anthropic introduced safeguards intended to prevent infringement. Requests to recreate songs for modern audiences allegedly produced versions retaining recognizable elements of the originals. Claude is an impressive assistant, but its ability to answer questions doesn't suddenly make songwriters' copyright interests irrelevant. An AI model learning about music isn't automatically infringing copyright, and copyright law doesn't give anyone ownership of an entire musical style. But if a commercial AI system reproduces protected lyrics or creates unauthorized adaptations, it's hard to see why the company behind it should get a special exemption simply because the copying happens through complicated software. AI companies have been trying out various arguments in court, but a lot of it feels like an attempt to claim that AI development is so important that the usual rules should somehow bend around it. Training requires enormous amounts of information, and licensing everything would be expensive or inconvenient, but that's a standard headache for companies whose products rely on copyrighted material. (Image credit: Warner Bros) TV shows and movies license music, whether an original track or just the right to record a new version for their project. No company is allowed to simply grab hold of copyrighted material simply because clearing it would slow down development. AI companies should have to take copyright seriously too, even if that makes their business models more expensive. It's also particularly galling that songs people spent years creating and popularizing can become raw material for commercial technology without the rights holders having any meaningful say. Access to a work and permission to exploit it are separate questions, regardless of how sophisticated the software becomes. Ignoring those rules is why artists who passed away decades ago seem to produce new music whose earnings don't go to their estate. AI music turns the volume up Elvis is hardly the first musician to become part of this fight. articles.title: New Apple TV 4K and iPad Mini: RAM Amounts Revealed
articles.content: Apple today released Xcode 27.2, and it reveals how much RAM is in the new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K and the new iPad mini with an OLED display . As expected, the new Apple TV 4K with the A19 chip is equipped with 8GB of RAM, while the new iPad mini with the A20 Pro chip has 12GB of RAM. For good measure, Xcode shows the iPhone Duo is equipped with 12GB of RAM. None of these RAM amounts are surprising, but Apple does not list this information in its tech specs for these devices, so they are worth confirming. An industrywide memory chip shortage has led to skyrocketing prices for RAM and storage chips, resulting in Apple raising prices this year across many products, including iPhones, iPads, Macs, HomePods, the Apple TV 4K, and more. articles.title: Google confirms: Fix is in the works for Pixel Watch extreme battery drain issue
articles.content: TL;DR Pixel Watch owners have been complaining about their battery life suddenly taking a nose dive. Multiple generations of watches have been impacted, making this look like a software issue, rather than hardware failure. Google now confirms that it’s identified the problem, and is developing a fix. Smartwatches are great, but battery life continues to be a problem. Sure, they can do a lot, but what good is all that potential if there’s no charge left when we go to use them? Things can be dicey enough when our watches are behaving as they should, but this week we learned about a new problem that seemed to be affecting Pixel Watch models , dropping battery life from the normal day or two we’re used to, down to just 12 hours. Thankfully, a fix is already in the works. Multiple reports from owners spanning from the Pixel Watch 2 up to the current generation all shared similar tales: battery life diving even as the watches sat idle. Disabling the Always-on Display didn’t seem to make much of an impact.

articles.title: Researchers find bugs in 5 AI developer tools, with OpenAI and Microsoft flaws still unpatched
articles.content: Multiple vulnerabilities in five popular AI developer tools could allow attackers to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof browser address bars. Researchers say flaws in OpenAI's Codex and Microsoft's VS Code remain unpatched, potentially putting developers who use affected configurations at risk. AI security startup Forever Security discovered vulnerabilities in Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Anthropic's Claude Desktop, VS Code, and Codex, and disclosed four of the flaws to the affected vendors. GitHub independently fixed the Copilot vulnerability without receiving a report from Forever Security. All five share a common security weakness: embedded browsers granted capabilities beyond those available to conventional browsers. Each tool “enriched its embedded browser beyond what a normal browser allows, and those enrichments undermined the traditional threat model - as agent input, as the authority on a tab’s own address, or as reach onto the host,” Forever researcher Gal Weizman wrote in a Thursday report . Forever dubbed this class of vulnerability “Embrace,” short for EMbedded BRowser, and said the flaws led to code execution in Cursor, data theft in Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code, and address bar spoofing in GitHub Copilot. Here’s what each of these looks like, starting with Cursor. Cursor: arbitrary code execution Typical web pages can’t run commands on the host computer because a web page’s JavaScript cannot talk to local apps. Cursor’s integrated browser, however, allows a page to call the agent’s composer. The agent reads this as instructions and follows them, but the instructions remain hidden from human users. This opens the coding agent up to prompt injection attacks that could allow an attacker to execute commands on the host machine. The researchers disclosed the vulnerability to Cursor on September 10, and the vendor silently patched the flaw on October 1. According to Forever, Cursor did not publish a security advisory about the issue or respond to the researchers' disclosure. Cursor also did not reply to The Register ’s request for comment. GitHub Copilot: address bar spoofing Under normal browser operations, a webpage cannot change the content of the address bar. “Copilot’s browser preview works differently,” Weizman wrote. “Some pages change their address without loading a new page, and the app cannot always see that. So Copilot let the page tell the app its own address.” The app checked only whether the text looked like a web address, starting with http, https or file, but it didn’t check where the tab really pointed to. This can be abused to trick the embedded browser into displaying a spoofed URL - such as github.com/login - in the address bar, while loading a fraudulent website - like a phishing page - underneath. The researchers found the address-bar spoofing flaw in GitHub Copilot 1.1.27 on September 26. GitHub independently fixed the flaw in a later Copilot build (1.1.29) on October 13 without receiving a vulnerability report from Forever. We reached out to GitHub and did not receive a response. Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code: arbitrary file read All three of these vendors’ coding assistants allow local HTML files opened in the built-in browser to escape its boundaries and access other files. Both Claude Desktop and VS Code allow local pages access to their respective project folders, but the researchers found that these restrictions did not apply to web workers – a browser feature that allows JavaScript to run in a background thread, separate from the page's main thread. This means a local page can start a worker, and the worker can bypass restrictions to reach any file on the machine. Codex, however, didn’t have this same restriction, meaning a local page could read any file directly without a worker. Weizman said his team disclosed the issue to Anthropic on July 23, and the AI vendor declined the Claude Desktop bug report as invalid for a “workspace trust” gated security…
articles.author: Jessica Lyons

articles.title: Trump's CTFC Steps In to Defend Kalshi As Utah Brings Criminal Charges Against Execs
articles.content: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has sued Utah to defend its claimed exclusive authority over federally registered prediction markets, as the state files (PDF) 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and its co-founders for allegedly violating anti-gambling laws. The Verge reports: On Wednesday, Utah's Attorney General Derek Brown filed charges against Kalshi co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, including 12 counts of online gambling promotion, a third-degree felony, one count of a pattern of unlawful activity, a second-degree felony, and general gambling promotion, a Class A misdemeanor. The civil lawsuit calls Kalshi a "back-alley gambling den," and Attorney General Brown didn't mince words in a statement to Gizmodo. "Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a 'prediction market' doesn't change what it is, and being federally registered doesn't put a company above the law," said Brown. "A federal court has already ruled that Utah's gambling laws apply to Kalshi," continued Brown. "Kalshi kept taking bets from Utahns anyway. That is illegal, and we're putting a stop to it." [...] The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has been jumping into action to protect Kalshi and Polymarket by filing lawsuits against any state that brings charges against the betting sites. President Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr., is a paid advisor to both companies. The CFTC announced Wednesday that it was suing the state of Utah as part of its "commitment to maintaining its exclusive jurisdiction over CFTC-registered prediction markets." The argument is that the feds alone should be regulating these sites. "Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets," CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig said in a statement. "Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes -- they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets," continued Selig. "As I've said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that's exactly what we'll do." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Sam Altman almost scrapped token pricing. Here’s why he backed off.
articles.content: OpenAI considered dropping token-based pricing for its next model , letting developers submit a prompt and receive a price for the work, before negative customer feedback convinced the company to back away from the idea, CEO Sam Altman says. The flat-fee pricing idea Speaking Thursday with Stripe President John Collison on the Cheeky Pint podcast, Altman recalls that OpenAI “almost made a very — what would’ve been a bad call” to stop pricing its next model in tokens altogether, moving instead to an arrangement where a developer hands over a prompt and OpenAI hands back a price. The billing would have worked “like AWS,” he explained, where you “just do something and we send you a bill” rather than metering the exchange token by token. Altman does not name the model in question or give a timeline for when the change was under consideration. We’ve cued up the exchange in the video below: Why customers pushed back The idea ran into resistance when OpenAI tried to gauge how customers felt about receiving a price with no breakdown. “The customer response on that is so negative,” Altman recounts, with buyers telling the company, “’I need to know what I’m paying for somehow.’” “’I need to know what I’m paying for somehow.’” Developers already spend plenty of time tracking input and output tokens to keep costs down and estimate what they’ll spend as usage grows. Getting a price without knowing how it was calculated would only make that harder. Paying more for clarity What makes the admission worth a second look is that, according to Altman, the people he consulted would rather pay more to keep that visibility. He put the question to “a few people,” asking whether they would take a higher rate for the same output as long as it stayed priced in consistent tokens, and the answer, he said, was that they would “much rather you inflate the tokens and pay more,” because “I know there’s a real thing there.” “much rather you inflate the tokens and pay more … I know there’s a real thing there.” Developers resist a single opaque price, he reasons, because they suspect that over the long run they are “gonna get screwed somehow,” the same instinct that once had buyers paying for CPU hours instead of for a finished job. The proposal could have had significant implications for developers building agents, whose multistep workflows already consume unpredictable amounts of compute and make spending difficult to forecast even under today’s token-based model. Altman does not explain how OpenAI would have set those per-job prices, or whether customers could have weighed one charge against another. Tokens, a ‘fake unit’ The subject came up when Collison pressed Altman on whether tokens were the right way to measure AI usage. Altman acknowledged the limitations of token pricing but had no clear alternative to offer. “Tokens are a kind of fake unit … they’re real in some sense, but they’re not a good unit.” “Tokens are a kind of fake unit,” he said. “I mean, they’re real in some sense, but they’re not a good unit.” He balked at Collison’s half-serious pitch to coin an intelligence-equivalent token, comparing it to the way chipmakers still market nanometer figures that no longer correspond to any physical measurement on the chip. Altman admits developers incur real overhead when choosing between a cheaper model and a more capable one , especially when they also have to guess how much reasoning a given task will demand. “That’s just cognitive overhead that I don’t think actually adds any value,” he said. articles.title: Tech Moves: Former Amazon execs depart Warner Bros. Discovery; Amazon leader returns to Microsoft
articles.content: Avi Saxena, left, and Tyler Whitworth. (LinkedIn Photos) — Two former Amazon executives who helped build Discovery ’s direct-to-consumer operation in Bellevue, Wash., are stepping down from their leadership roles following the company’s acquisition by Paramount Skydance. They will remain in advisory roles during the transition. Avi Saxena joined Discovery in 2019 as chief technology officer of its direct-to-consumer business and led its new Bellevue office. He became CTO of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) following Discovery’s 2022 merger with AT&T’s WarnerMedia business. Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of WBD on Oct. 6, with the combined company taking the name Skydance Corporation. Before joining Discovery, Saxena was with Amazon for 19 years over two stints, most recently as vice president of technology for Amazon Marketplace. He also held leadership roles at Microsoft and internet infrastructure startups. Tyler Whitworth is stepping down as executive vice president and chief product officer for WBD’s streaming business. He led teams working on digital products for HBO Max, discovery+, Eurosport, TNT Sports, Food Network and others. Before joining Discovery, he spent more than seven years at Amazon, leading teams developing products and services for customers and third-party sellers. Dane Glasgow, Skydance’s chief product officer, announced the departures of Whitworth, Saxena and WBD Chief Information Officer Dave Duvall in a memo shared with GeekWire. “Much of the strength of WBD’s product and technology organizations reflects their leadership and dedication. Please join me in thanking them and wishing them the very best,” Glasgow wrote. The company has not responded to GeekWire’s inquiries about the future of the Bellevue office. Bahadir Onalan. (LinkedIn Photo) — Bahadir Onalan is returning to Microsoft as a vice president in its CoreAI organization, focused on responsible AI, after nearly 10 years at Amazon. Onalan first joined Microsoft in 2005 and worked on Azure teams focused on search, analytics, business intelligence and security. He left in 2017 as a principal software group engineering manager to join Amazon, where he worked on machine learning initiatives. “This second tenure feels like a true homecoming,” Onalan wrote . “Our goal goes beyond shipping a platform or a product; we are here to define the global standards for AI safety.” Naria Santa Lucia. (LinkedIn Photo) — Naria Santa Lucia is leaving Microsoft after seven years, most recently as a general manager with Microsoft Elevate. She previously served as executive director of the Washington State Opportunity Scholarship. “I’ll carry the lessons I learned from my time at Microsoft as I continue my personal and professional mission to serve people and communities by teaching, advising nonprofits and mission driven organizations, and spreading joy and human connection,” Santa Lucia wrote . She did not announce a specific next role. Leo Ochoa, left, and Aina Abiodun. (LinkedIn Photos) — VertueLab , a Pacific Northwest nonprofit supporting climate tech entrepreneurs, has named Leo Ochoa executive director, promoting him from managing director for Oregon. He succeeds Aina Abiodun , who is transitioning to chair of the organization’s board after more than three years as executive director. “Leo brings a unique blend of vision, relationships, and entrepreneurship experience,” the organization said , noting his background as a wildland firefighter, startup founder and patent holder for wearable safety gear. Abiodun’s accomplishments include co-creating the Seattle Climate Innovation Hub, launching the Opalene Climate Challenge and helping lead the Just Future Climate Labs initiative. Leah Sardone. (LinkedIn Photo) — Seattle’s Pulse Space has appointed Leah Sardone as vice president of engineering. The startup is developing laser-based systems to deliver power and enable long-distance communications in low Earth orbit…

"Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating," said Binance on X. "User funds are safe," said Binance founder CZ. "It does look like a hack on Binance. articles.title: Intel confirms Nova Lake CPUs will use advanced 18A-P node, more details at CES — company says it's taking Panther Lake capacity offline to build more Granite Rapids data center CPUs
articles.content: Intel's next-gen Nova Lake desktop processors will be the first client product to use Intel's enhanced 18A-P node, CEO Lip-Bu Tan confirmed in the company's Q3 2026 earnings call. The chief executive also said that the company intends to share more about Nova Lake at CES in January. The company's chief financial officer shared that Intel intends to take Panther Lake capacity offline to build more Granite Rapids data center CPUs. Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platforms CPU scaling with DLSS Intel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shape Benchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the price AMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent "Nova Lake, our first Intel 18A-P client product, is tracking ahead of schedule, with design wins expecting to be twice those of Panther Lake at launch," Tan said in his prepared remarks. "We look forward to sharing more at CES in January." There has been a lot of speculation about what node Intel's Nova Lake CPUs will use, with the rumor mill ping-ponging between Intel 18A and TSMC's N2P. Current speculation says the chip will use 18A-P for the SoC tile while using TSMC's N2P for the compute tile. It seems unlikely that Intel would use its most advanced node for an SoC tile, though it's possible. Regardless, Nova Lake chips will use 18A-P in some regard. Intel announced in June that 18A-P had entered risk production , and at Hot Chips in August, Intel revealed its next-gen Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids will be the company's first server products to use the enhanced node. Compared to 18A, which is available in Panther Lake and Wildcat Lake products currently, 18A-P comes with a 9% improvement in speed at iso-power, or an 18% reduction in power at iso-speed. Intel has described 18A-P as a drop-in replacement for 18A, allowing designs built for 18A to instead leverage 18A-P without any extra engineering work. For 18A products, Intel says its new Wildcat Lake products that have shown up in devices like the Framework Laptop 12 are increasingly popular. "Demand for our Wildcat Lake is outstripping supply," said Tan. Intel says that 18A products now make up a third of client CPU revenue, up from less than 5% in Q1. It makes sense that those products would be popular given the current environment. Tan said that Intel's OEM partners are "aggressively managing inventory to match softer sell-through," which means buying less to match the demand in the market. Intel's David Zinsner said the company expects the company's client business to decline by "more than 20%" in the next quarter." Zinsner warned of a further contraction in the PC market, describing a sustained decline in the size of the market over the next year, at least. "We expect the 2026 PC unit [Total Addressable Market] to decline approximately 12%, with second half units down more than 20%. We do not expect a sustained recovery until memory availability improves and pricing begins to normalize," Zinsner said. "For 2027, we're planning a PC unit TAM to decline roughly 10%." Taking the comments together, Intel is saying that it expects the market itself to shrink significantly over the next year due to memory prices. It's not a situation of demand outstripping supply, at least not directly like the case of a component shortage. Rather, it's a pullback from direct customers, OEMs, and IT departments from spending, which is more significant. Although Intel says the client PC market is shrinking, the company says that its long-term outlook remains positive. "We think next year, and in future years, we're a market-share-gain type of environment... we do think the PC is going to through a renaissance despite [memory shortage]," said Zinsner. articles.title: AWS’s Hydro team wants the compiler to catch coding agents’ mistakes
articles.content: Earlier this month, the team behind Hydro developed a new way to check that a distributed system still works correctly when it resends messages after a failure. This produced what Shadaj Laddad described to me as “like a 5000 line PR.” Hydro is an open-source Rust framework for distributed systems, the software that runs across many machines at once, and agents now write most of it with humans driving. The PR was difficult to split into smaller pieces as its components worked together. That’s a lot of code to review for a tool developers count on to catch bugs. Laddad, research lead for the Hydro team at AWS, says it’s something the team spends a lot of time thinking about. I sat down with him last week at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose. He was set to give a keynote the next day where he was going to argue code review can’t keep pace with how agents write code. Agents have let the team aim higher, Laddad told me, saying PRs arrive faster and run longer. “You can have the feature work well in isolation, then you mix it with something else, and suddenly the guarantees break down,” he said. And you can’t just trust the tests. In most agent workflows, he says, the agent writes both the code and the unit tests. “Agents are great, but they’re unpredictable,” Laddad said. That unpredictability is part of what makes them creative, and it makes it hard for a human to review all those tests and confirm they do what the team wants. His answer is shared Correctness checks outside the agent’s “zone of trust,” such as those enforced by a compiler. Rust’s borrow checker is his example: It catches race conditions before the code ever runs. Hydro does something similar for distributed systems, catching several types of bugs at compile time so an agent gets instant feedback on mistakes it introduced. The wider goal, which the team is still exploring, is domain-specific guardrails that agents can share. To find candidates, the team studies historical projects for recurring patterns. Idempotency, ensuring a retried request doesn’t run twice, comes up repeatedly in design reviews, so the team is asking whether it can become a general-purpose guardrail. Laddad sees this as the next rung on an old ladder. C spared programmers from mangling function calls in assembly. Java took memory allocation off their plate. Agents, he argued, make the next layer more urgent. Compilers have limits, though. As The New Stack reported in August, AI-generated Rust can compile perfectly and still be wrong . The same team also built Infinity , an open-source agent runtime AWS announced on October 23. It suspends an agent while it waits on a tool call or a CI job instead of keeping it running. Laddad cited a benchmark showing 75,000 concurrent agents on a single Raspberry Pi. According to the AWS announcement, that figure is extrapolated from a server test in which each idle agent used about 100 KB. Hydro itself is an early release, built for teams running high-throughput, low-latency services who are constantly worried about distributed systems bugs. Laddad noted that users should expect rough edges and a learning curve right now. The payoff is the confidence to change a system without fearing it will break a few months later. Hydro and Infinity are open source at hydro.run , built jointly by AWS and UC Berkeley. The post AWS’s Hydro team wants the compiler to catch coding agents’ mistakes appeared first on The New Stack .

articles.content: In the future, you won’t be able to use Reddit without logging in. Reddit CEO Steve Huffman confirmed the impending change in a letter (PDF) to shareholders today about Q3 performance. He said that Reddit is shifting “to a logged-in-only experience," adding: Moving to primarily logged-in will ensure our users have the best Reddit experience possible, and can find the content and communities most relevant to them. It is better for our business because we will have more signals for ads targeting, and being logged-in leads to higher engagement generally. It also allows us to protect access to Reddit’s extremely valuable corpus of data, and helps us better adapt to emerging regulations around the world. Huffman also said that the login requirement will help Reddit better retain new users. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Your Billing Migration is Really a State Machine
articles.content: A customer opens their inbox and finds two invoices for the same subscription. Another customer shows up in the retention report as a churn, except they never cancelled. Their payment failed, the subscription lapsed in the billing system, and the lapse got recorded as a lost customer. I led the architecture on a migration that produced both of these bugs. A large file-sharing company was replacing its homegrown quoting and billing system with Salesforce CPQ and Salesforce Billing, integrated with Oracle ERP, across hundreds of thousands of customer accounts. The data moved fine. State was the problem. First, A Little About Me I’m Naresh Goyal, a Salesforce and GTM systems architect with 20+ years in CPQ, billing, and revenue systems. I hold the Revenue Cloud Advanced certification and led the architecture on the migration in this story. Alongside revenue systems work, I've been focused on bringing AI into go-to-market teams. I led AI deployment across a GTM organization, built an AI orchestration platform for revenue workflows, and set up a Salesforce MCP integration with Claude so agents can work directly with CRM data. That work keeps reinforcing the same lesson as this migration: AI agents are only as reliable as the state they read. I’m sharing these lessons because billing migrations usually fail quietly, and most fixes only surface in postmortems. Your subscription state lives in four places at once. A subscription does not live in one system. Quoting knows what was sold. Billing knows what was invoiced and paid. Provisioning knows what the customer can access. The ERP knows what revenue was recognized. Each system holds a partial copy of the truth, and each one updates on its own schedule. When those copies disagree, the bug lands on a customer. Billing treats a subscription as active and keeps invoicing it after provisioning has shut off access. Or the reverse. The failures we kept hitting were duplicate invoices for one subscription, churn records for customers whose only problem was a failed payment, and provisioning that fired at the wrong moment, granting access before payment was confirmed or withholding it after. None of these are data movement bugs. The records arrived. They arrived carrying state that the receiving system read differently. Write the state machine down before you configure anything. Our fix started on a whiteboard. Every subscription got an explicit state machine: named states and the allowed transitions between them. Draft, quoted, ordered, activated, suspended, amended, expired, cancelled. A subscription could move from ordered to activated. It could not jump from quoted to invoiced, and any process that tried got rejected instead of quietly writing a bad state. This sounds basic, and most billing systems never do it. State ends up implied by a status field here, a checkbox there, a date that may or may not be set. When state is implied, every integration invents its own reading of it, and you ship the disagreements to your customers. Here is a simplified version of the transition table. The important column is the last one. From To Trigger Owning system Draft Quoted Quote generated Quoting (CPQ) Quoted Ordered Quote accepted Quoting (CPQ) Ordered Activated Order recognized by finance Billing Activated Suspended Payment failed Billing Suspended Activated Payment recovered Billing Suspended Cancelled Dunning exhausted Billing Activated Amended Upsell or downgrade quoted Quoting (CPQ) Amended Activated Amendment order recognized Billing Activated Expired Term ends without renewal Billing Activated Cancelled Customer cancels Quoting (CPQ) Notice that "payment failed" moves a subscription to Suspended, not Cancelled. That row addresses the false churn problem from the opening. Churn reporting counts Cancelled and Expired, never Suspended, so a failed card no longer looks like a lost customer. Do this on your own migration: list the states, list the transitions, and name the one system allowed to…

articles.title: Google is cleaning up Home’s messiest bugs, with fixes for cameras, Matter devices, and more
articles.content: TL;DR Google is updating the Home app and Gemini with all its latest smart home fixes. Gemini should no longer complain about misunderstanding commands you never issued. A number of fixes aim to resolve performance problems with cameras in the app. As anyone who has seriously built up a household around Google Home can attest to, the service can feel like it’s constantly in a state of flux. New fixes are arriving all the time, and today Google just shared word of a big wave of updates arriving for the company’s hardware. But that’s just the half of it, and Google’s also telling us about the latest improvements coming to Gemini and the Google Home app. Google published an almost overwhelming Home changelog earlier today, detailing the past couple weeks’ worth of fixes and upgrades. Some of these read a little familiar, like promises for Gemini to understand us better — and here, specifically, Google’s putting a stop to devices blurting out “sorry, I didn’t understand,” in response to nothing at all.

articles.title: Baseten Releases joey-1, a 2B Decision Model at $0.01 per 1M Tokens
articles.content: Baseten has released joey-1 , a 2B model from its in-house research lab, Base Labs. The joey-1 decision model returns a label and a calibrated probability instead of generated text. It targets high-volume routing, classification and guardrail checks. Baseten prices it at $0.01 per million input tokens , with open weights on Hugging Face under MIT. TL;DR Size: 2B parameters, post-trained from Qwen3.5-2B. 16,384-token max sequence (Baseten says 262k on dedicated deployments). Runs on: Baseten Model APIs, or self-hosted on 1 CUDA GPU (VRAM not disclosed). No official quantized builds listed. Performance: Top model under 4B on the Jev Decision Index 0.4 public split, per Baseten. Best: 63.30 on Jev Decision Index 0.4 (public split), ranked #37 of 230 models. Worst: Trails its 9B sibling elephant-1 by 8.94 points on the same split (63.30 vs 72.24). Bottom line: Best: 20 ms P50 decisions for $0.01 per 1M tokens. Worst: less general knowledge than its larger siblings. What is joey-1? joey-1 is a 2B decision model from Baseten’s Base Labs that answers typed questions in 1 forward pass. You send a state (text or images) and 1 or more questions. The model returns a probability for every option of every question. It does not write free-form text that your application must parse. It supports 3 question types: choice: pick 1 named option, such as which team owns a ticket. yes/no ( noul in the API): returns the probability of yes. score: ordered levels, lowest first, such as urgency. joey-1 is the third member of a family. Baseten shipped mammoth-1 (27B) and elephant-1 (9B) last week. All 3 share training data and the /v1/systemone API, so switching is a 1-line change. How does joey-1 work? Base Labs post-trained Qwen3.5-2B with a full fine-tune of the language model. The vision encoder stays frozen. Full-attention layers use a block-bidirectional mask. All questions are answered from 1 shared-prefix prefill, so extra questions add little cost. Training details from the model card : Data: 6.21M decision examples. Mix: 58.3% core decision skills, 16.1% safety, 16.1% judging and expert domains, 9.5% public data. Objective: cross-entropy plus a Brier calibration term, with a trained “I don’t know” option. Recipe: 1 epoch, 43,390 steps, peak learning rate 1e-5, bf16. Hardware: 2 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. Calibration lets you set a confidence threshold. Uncertain answers can escalate to elephant-1, mammoth-1 or a human. How fast and cheap is joey-1? Baseten reports a P50 end-to-end latency of 20 ms for an average 2,000-token request. That is about 2.5x faster than elephant-1 (49 ms). The blog’s TL;DR also claims 5x faster than comparable decision models, without naming them. Model APIs charge $0.01 per 1M input tokens; output and cached input are listed at $0.00. elephant-1 costs $0.035 and mammoth-1 costs $0.10. Baseten’s example: 10M support tickets a month at about 500 tokens each is 5B tokens. That is about $50 on joey-1, versus $500 on mammoth-1. How does joey-1 score on benchmarks? All scores below are self-reported on Baseten’s model card . On the Jev Decision Index 0.4 public split, joey-1 scores 63.30. That ranks #37 of 230 models and is the top score under 4B. The Jev Decision Index is a community leaderboard on Hugging Face. On the same split, Cloudflare’s 27B Clef scores 61.71 and Jev 1.14 scores 60.70. joey-1 trails elephant-1 in every area. It beats Jev 1.14 in 4 of 5 areas, including language, tools and retrieval. On Baseten’s replica of the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, joey-1 scores 62.9, versus 65.9 for mammoth-1. joey-1 vs. other small decision models Feature joey-1 elephant-1 Perplexity Decider Flash v1.2 Cloudflare Clef-Flash Developer Baseten (Base Labs) Baseten (Base Labs) Perplexity Cloudflare Parameters 2B 9B 4B 9B Base model Qwen3.5-2B Qwen3.5-9B Qwen3.5-4B Qwen3.5-9B License MIT MIT Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Inputs Text, images Text, images Text, images Text, JSON,…

articles.title: Apple Executive Comments on New iPad Mini Lacking 120Hz Display
articles.content: While the new iPad mini has an OLED display, the device does not support ProMotion, meaning the display's refresh rate is limited to 60Hz instead of 120Hz. ProMotion support would have allowed for the iPad mini's refresh rate to automatically adjust from 10Hz to 120Hz depending on the content being displayed, but evidently Apple has kept the feature exclusive to the iPad Pro among iPad models for now. In an interview with YouTuber and podcaster Christopher Lawley, Apple's vice president of hardware design David Pakula commented on the new iPad mini lacking 120Hz support, noting that its OLED display still has significantly faster pixel response times compared to the previous model with an LCD, resulting in reduced motion blur. "Display experience is about more than just a single spec," said Pakula. "One of the things that's really cool about OLED is it actually has this really fast pixel response time. So it's like more than an order of magnitude faster than the pixel response time for an LCD display. And what that does is it makes everything really smooth. Motion blur is significantly reduced compared to LCD. When you pair that with the other things that I mentioned, the contrast, the brightness, and the color, this is just a killer display." Apple says the new iPad mini can achieve a maximum brightness of 600 nits for standard content, up from 500 nits for the previous model, and up to 1,200 nits for HDR content. OLED technology allows for higher contrast and more vivid colors, as there is no backlight and individual pixels turn off completely to display true black. Apple's tech specs indicate the new iPad mini has a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The display still has 326 pixels per inch and P3 wide color support. The new iPad mini is available to pre-order now , with U.S. pricing starting at $699, and the device launches on Friday, November 6. articles.title: Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek' Captain and 'X-Men' Superhero, Dies At 86
articles.content: Slashdot readers Cpt_Kirks, eklektic, sconeu, and Vrallis share the unfortunate news of Patrick Stewart's passing. Longtime spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said Stewart died Wednesday at the age of 86 at his home in Los Angeles following "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia." "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Bush Novak wrote. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace." The acclaimed British actor became a science-fiction icon as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films. Beyond those iconic roles, Stewart earned multiple Emmy and Golden Globe nominations for performances in Moby Dick, The Lion in Winter, Extras, Hamlet, and Blunt Talk. He later returned to his most famous role in Star Trek: Picard. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: The Zombies of Tech: What Actually Powers the World
articles.content: In Week 9 of the IBM Full-Stack JavaScript Developer track, I stepped back from tutorials and asked a different question: what is the internet actually running on? The answer isn’t the framework that trended on X this morning. It’s older, quieter, and far more stubborn. COBOL: the 67-year-old that moves your money. Created in 1959, COBOL is still widely estimated to sit behind about 95% of ATM transactions and 80% of in-person banking transactions, with some 220 billion lines in production and around $3 trillion in commerce a day. One example: back in 2012, Bank of New York Mellon reported maintaining 112,500 COBOL programs, about 343 million lines of code. The catch is a talent gap. Universities largely stopped teaching it decades ago, and banks are now experimenting with AI tools to help maintain and modernize it. PHP and WordPress: the web’s workhorse. PHP is used by about 70% of websites whose server-side language is known. WordPress, built on it, runs roughly 42% of all websites. jQuery: declared dead, still everywhere. It’s on about 67% of all websites. Even jQuery 1.x, a version from the 2000s, is still found on around 13%. Linux: the invisible foundation. About 62% of websites with an identifiable OS run Linux, and the broader Unix family covers around 92%. Every system on the TOP500 supercomputer list runs Linux too. And the new stuff earns its place. React Native isn’t legacy, but it shows why tools survive: Shopify moved its flagship app to it and now shares about 86% of its code across iOS and Android, up from roughly 5%. Efficiency like that is why a tool lasts. My takeaway: the technologies that last aren’t the newest; they’re the ones that are reliable, and rewriting something that works is expensive and risky. As a developer, learning the new tools matters, but so does respecting the old systems that keep running. What’s the oldest piece of tech you’ve seen still running in production? Sources: W3Techs (2026), Reuters (2017), Computerworld (2012), Shopify’s React Native migration. Usage figures cover only sites where the technology is detectable.

articles.title: Microsoft’s new Copilot harness makes agents easy — until you want to switch
articles.content: Microsoft is opening up the GitHub Copilot agent harness to outside developers through Microsoft Foundry, bringing the same orchestration infrastructure used across its Copilot products into a managed service for building and deploying autonomous agents. Announced Wednesday , the Microsoft Copilot harness is now available in public preview through Foundry Agent Service. It comes with built-in sandboxing, reusable skills, MCP integrations, and support for subagents. Microsoft takes care of running the agent and managing its execution environment, leaving developers to choose a supported model and configure the instructions and tools for their applications. The same harness now supports Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, GitHub Copilot, the CLI, and VS Code. The company is also using GitHub’s agent infrastructure across more of its Copilot products. It’s a continuation of the Foundry strategy outlined at Build 2026 , which focuses on making AI agents easier for companies to run, manage, and control. The same harness now supports Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, GitHub Copilot, the CLI, and VS Code. Inside the managed Copilot harness Microsoft’s harness manages model and tool calls, tracks context, and keeps agents within configured policies. Skills can package instructions, scripts, and supporting resources, while MCP integrations require authentication and approval. Agents can also work with files, run code, and delegate tasks to subagents, with the main agent coordinating the results. Microsoft’s harness manages model and tool calls, tracks context, and keeps agents within configured policies. How developers deploy agents The company’s technical walkthrough shows how this works with a research agent. A Markdown-based skill lays out the steps for collecting evidence, analyzing data, and writing a report, while an azure.yaml file defines the model deployment, tools, instructions, and harness. Developers select microsoft_copilot_preview as the harness type, deploy the agent using azd deploy --all and invoke it through the Azure Developer CLI. They can keep agent configurations and supporting files in source control, making it easier to track changes alongside their application code. Runtime limits and lock-in The Copilot harness must be selected when creating a prompt agent, and that choice can’t be changed later, even in a new version. Microsoft also controls how much CPU and memory the agent gets and how long it can sit idle. Developers can decide what their agents do, but have less control over the environment they run in. Developers can decide what their agents do, but have less control over the environment they run in. Microsoft is positioning its broader harness strategy as multi-model, although there are limits. Developers can choose from compatible models deployed through Foundry, but bringing their own models isn’t supported with the managed Copilot harness. Teams that want more control can use Foundry’s hosted agents instead. Teams can build and run agents using their own frameworks and customize how they operate, while Microsoft handles the hosting. The company also announced general availability of long-running resilience for hosted agents on Wednesday, helping them recover from interruptions during tasks that take hours or even days to complete. Foundry agent pricing explained The Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service for free until December 1, 2026, although model inference and some tools and connected services still come with separate charges. After that, Microsoft will charge $0.0994 per vCPU-hour for compute and $0.0118 per GiB-hour for memory. Those rates may vary depending on the region and customer agreement. articles.title: Apple Avoids Showing Pinched Fingers on iPad Mini Page in South Korea
articles.content: In the U.S. and most other countries, Apple's website shows the new iPad mini being held by pinched fingers, but this is not the case in South Korea. The new iPad mini shown with pinched fingers on Apple's website in the U.S. On its South Korean website , Apple simply shows an image of the iPad mini on its own. The new iPad mini shown without pinched fingers on Apple's website in South Korea Apple also omitted the pinched fingers from its South Korean website for the iPhone Air in 2025, but they remain visible on its U.S. website . In South Korea, a pinched-fingers gesture or emoji has reportedly been interpreted by some as a symbol used to mock the size of men's genitals. Apple has not commented on this matter. articles.title: Beyond Price, What Gives Bitcoin Its Value?
articles.content: Bitcoin began its history back in the distant 2008–2009. During this time, it managed to transform from an obscure digital currency that was once used to buy pizza into a highly liquid asset. Although the basic principles of Bitcoin have remained the same, its price has changed dramatically during this period. Just a year ago, in October 2025, one BTC was worth about $126,080. And a year later, at the end of October 2026, its price fell by almost 36% — to $81,000. Such “ups and downs” are an interesting phenomenon for me as the CEO of a crypto aggregator. Bitcoin became the starting point for the development of the modern crypto industry, and its price movements influence the mood and dynamics of the entire market. In this article, I’ll look beyond the price chart to explore what gives Bitcoin its value, what drives demand for BTC, and why its role in the crypto market goes far beyond its latest price movements. * Value and price answer different questions The value of Bitcoin is an individual story. For example, two different people may explain what it consists of in different ways. Someone doesn’t want to use traditional banks for payments or transfers and therefore uses Bitcoin. For another person, it’s more important to have a “reliable” crypto asset with a history and limited supply in their crypto portfolio. These cases are small illustrations of how Bitcoin can be used and what it’s valued for. But value and price are different things. The quoted price is just the price that the buyer and seller come to in each individual trade. One seller takes what the buyer offers, and the next trade may be at a different price. There is no hidden agreed value in dollars behind the quote that you're meant to be able to work out. Thus, it is more difficult to evaluate Bitcoin than a traditional financial asset. Unlike stocks, Bitcoin does not entitle you to any future earnings of a company, nor are there any future cash flows that can be used to determine its value. According to Fidelity, crypto valuation is all about supply and demand. However, that doesn't provide a clear 'fair value' figure. What supports Bitcoin's value 1. Predictable issuance Since 2012, Bitcoin has undergone a halving approximately every four years, reducing the block subsidy by 50% every 210,000 blocks. Following the April 2024 halving, the subsidy fell to 3.125 BTC per block, down from the initial 50 BTC. What does this tell us? Bitcoin has a capped supply of approximately 21 million coins, while the rate of new BTC issuance declines with each halving. However, as Eswar Prasad argues in his article, The Brutal Truth About Bitcoin , scarcity alone is unlikely to be a sufficient source of value. I agree with this view. In my opinion, a more significant feature is the predictability of Bitcoin’s issuance schedule . The block subsidy is determined by the protocol rules and block height, rather than by the discretionary decisions of a centralized issuer. Anyone considering buying BTC can examine these rules to understand how the issuance of new coins is expected to change over time. This allows you to take halving into account when assessing the market, but it doesn’t allow you to predict price movements. A reduction in the rate of new BTC issuance alone doesn’t guarantee an increase in Bitcoin’s value: much depends on demand and other market factors. Therefore, when making a decision to buy, it’s important to consider not only the issuance rate but also the possible risks. Figure 2. Bitcoin block subsidy by issuance era (2009 to April 2024). BTC per block (excluding transaction fees). Sources: Bitcoin Core and CoinMarketCap halving history . 2. Decentralization and сontrol The Bitcoin blockchain is designed so that transactions and blocks are independently verified by network participants. Miners use Proof of Work to propose new blocks, while full nodes check whether those blocks comply with Bitcoin’s protocol rules. Proof of Work makes it costly to rewrite…

articles.title: AWS growth hits 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, as Amazon misses on earnings
articles.content: AWS now brings in revenue at a $184 billion annual pace, and it’s closing in on Amazon’s third-party seller business as the company’s second-largest source of sales. (GeekWire File Photo / Todd Bishop) Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter , its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects the cloud unit to top 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028. That wasn’t enough for investors. Amazon posted earnings of $1.89 per share, well short of the $1.97 analysts expected, as higher interest costs on its growing debt and other losses ate into its profit. Operating income beat expectations at $28.1 billion, above the high end of Amazon’s own guidance, and the 13.9% operating margin for the quarter was the highest in the company’s history. Revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12%, came in just under analyst estimates but at the top of Amazon’s forecast range. Shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading, after closing down 4% during the regular session. Update: On the earnings call, Jassy said AWS has a backlog of $578 billion in contracted future revenue, more than double a year earlier. He also said Amazon expects to spend “meaningfully more” on capital projects in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion it plans for this year. Amazon may need to count on its legendary willingness to be “misunderstood for long periods of time,” as it asks investors to look past the costs to where its biggest businesses are headed. In the company’s earnings release , Jassy said Amazon’s retail business is gaining market share with improving margins. Retail sales, including online stores, physical stores and third-party seller services, totaled nearly $500 billion over the past 12 months, and AWS is now at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate. “There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years,” he said. On the earnings call, Jassy said those two businesses are AWS and Amazon’s stores business. Advertising grew 11% to $19.6 billion, or 12% excluding currency changes, down from 22% on that basis a year earlier. Amazon blamed the timing of Prime Day and a few other factors, and said it expects ad growth to return to the high teens in the fourth quarter. Online stores grew 2% to $68.5 billion, held back by Prime Day moving into the second quarter this year. Amazon said overall revenue growth would have been about 4 percentage points higher without the shift. Third-party seller services , the fees Amazon collects from merchants on its site, grew 9% to $46.5 billion. AWS came within about $500 million of it. Subscription services , which includes Prime memberships, grew 11% to $14 billion. Physical stores , mostly Whole Foods, grew 2% to $5.7 billion. Outlook: Amazon expects fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, up 12% to 16%, and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion. Related Andy Jassy’s prediction: Amazon could have two $1 trillion businesses within a decade Wall Street had expected fourth-quarter operating income of $33.2 billion, near the top of that range, according to analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. It still expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year. Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the earnings call that costs for Amazon Leo, the company’s satellite internet service, are weighing on its fourth-quarter profit forecast as the service gets ready to launch later this year. Amazon’s free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier, mostly because of its AI investments.

articles.title: Adapting a SwiftUI Courier App for iPhone Duo's Foldable Display
articles.content: Our courier app launched on the iPhone Duo simulator but there was no back button on the Messages screen. The details sheet covered the navigation controls. On a map, part of the route could easily be out of view. These were gaps in our app. We wanted to fix them before marking the app ready for the Duo. Much of the work involved how our existing interface worked in a differently-shaped window. Once the map, sheets and navigation started to play well together, we could produce a screenshot of the app for the App Store in an unfolded state. In our driver screens we show a route on a map, delivery details, messages and actions for proof of delivery. On a narrow iPhone, a bottom sheet lets the driver switch between the details and the map. On the Duo, both could be shown at once. Opening the app was the beginning In this wider view, the relationship between the views changed. At times, the system would present the sheet next to the map. And navigation buttons could appear in a space occupied by the sheet. In the narrow view, we had assumptions about this layout. They no longer held up. We started this work using the iOS 27.1 Duo simulator and Xcode 27.1 beta tooling. The observations below are of that tooling, not necessarily of every release of Xcode or of every piece of Duo hardware. We didn't save the version of the beta build used to take our screenshots. You could check Apple's release notes for Xcode 27.1 and test for tooling issues in that version. Work out where the sheet actually is In our first pass at this, we used size classes to work out whether the sheet would be docked. In three places in our code we guessed at that. But a size class doesn't tell us where the sheet might end up. It's up to the system whether to present the sheet on one side of the map. We wanted the content of the sheet, the map and navigation to all agree on the layout. Instead of guessing, we took a measurement of the sheet and the map. And we compared the horizontal position of the sheet with the bounds of the map. struct SheetPlacement: Equatable { var map: ClosedRange<CGFloat>? var sheet: ClosedRange<CGFloat>? var isDocked: Bool { guard let map, let sheet else { return false } let width = map.upperBound - map.lowerBound return sheet.lowerBound - map.lowerBound > width / 4 && map.upperBound - sheet.upperBound < 32 } } Each view reports its frame through SwiftUI’s onGeometryChange modifier. We compare the horizontal bounds of the sheet and map to determine whether the sheet is docked. So if you pull up or down on a bottom sheet, our decision about whether to dock it doesn't change. Put the back button where the driver can reach it The thresholds support our sheet-and-map layout. They aren't part of a broader SwiftUI docking system. Most importantly, we now provided the same answer about the position of the sheet to each of the views involved. Most obviously, this broke Messages. In our unfolded state, we showed a rail on the trailing edge of the navigation bar. When the sheet docked, it covered this rail (including the back button). A screen can feel open, yet still be limiting for the user. We wanted the same map and navigation actions regardless of where the sheet appeared. When the sheet is docked, we hide the navigation bar. But we add those actions over the top-leading corner of the map. When the sheet returns to the bottom, we restore the normal navigation bar. .toolbar(placement.isDocked ? .hidden : .automatic, for: .navigationBar) .overlay(alignment: .topLeading) { if placement.isDocked { controls() .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading) .padding(.trailing, placement.trailingInset) } } This inset on the trailing edge represents how much of the screen the docked sheet would occupy. That way, the driver could see some of the map and the controls. And we made the controls respond to Dynamic Type. ViewThatFits first shows them in a single row. But as the available space shrinks, it pushes the actions on the map into a second row.…

articles.title: Microsoft fixes a Windows 11 annoyance as PC revenue declines
articles.content: Microsoft is beginning the rollout of a Windows 11 preview update that finally addresses a persistent power user complaint with the operating system: the right-click menu that obliterated years of muscle memory on command locations and hid others behind an additional click. The timing is notable, as the announcement comes alongside Microsoft's quarterly financial report, which showed a continued decline in the business of selling Windows licenses for new PCs. The preview update, KB5127936 , is cumulative for Windows 11 versions 26H2 and 25H2. The update will be a gradual rollout before eventually moving on to a normal rollout for all Windows 11 devices once it reaches general availability. The highlight of the new update should calm annoyed users who have spent years with custom scripts and services in an attempt to shape Windows the way they would prefer it. Users will get a "customize menu" button that controls what commands appear when they right-click their mouse. Users can toggle built-in commands such as Send To or Create Shortcut on or off, rearrange what appears on the main menu, and control which third-party extensions show up in either the main or submenus. The gripe with the right-click menu had been that Microsoft hid familiar command locations behind a top row of icons while moving other familiar commands under the "Show more options" submenu. Now, Windows users can customize the whole thing around their habits. The original Windows 11 right-click menu is a mess. Credit: Microsoft The new preview also highlights a new Windows feature called Cloud Rebuild, a recovery option that can reinstall Windows 11 directly from the cloud, even when an existing Windows 11 fails to boot. Cloud Rebuild will pull the Windows 11 image and needed system drivers directly from Windows Update. Users will not need a custom recovery image or external media to reinstall Windows. There is an important distinction to note, however. Microsoft classifies Cloud Rebuild as a recovery option, but it behaves more like a fresh Windows install than a repair, as existing applications and files will not be included. Those worried about data security can sanitize entire system drives prior to reinstalling. For a full list of improvements coming to Windows 11, including changes to Xbox mode and settings, you can view the official Microsoft release announcement . Read full article Comments

articles.title: It's Time for Generative AI to Prioritize Understanding Over Communication
articles.content: The human element of communication Past communication tech conquered physical distance and time. But as generative AI becomes part of how we create, receive, and interpret human messages, it must focus not just on speed and ease, but on reducing the emotional and interpretive distance between people. Communication is one of the most basic human survival behaviors. People communicate to warn others about danger, ask for help, share knowledge, coordinate actions, build relationships, solve conflicts, and make decisions. In modern society, almost every form of collective activity depends on communication: scientific research, business cooperation, education, government operations, family life, and even an ordinary conversation between friends. Therefore, communication has never been only about transmitting information. If communication were simply about moving information from Point A to Point B, then a fax machine would already have solved most human problems. Unfortunately, humans are not fax machines. The deeper purpose of communication is to meet human needs. We need to understand the environment around us, and we also need to understand the people around us. We want other people to understand our intentions, needs, and concerns. At the same time, we must work with people whose knowledge, interests, values, and life experiences may be completely different from our own. So communication looks simple, but in reality it is extremely complex. At the most basic level, the structure of communication is so simple: a sender creates a message, a medium carries it, and a receiver receives and interprets it. For decades, this has been one of the central structures in communication theory . The problem is that two sides of this process are human. And once human beings are involved, things are no longer simple. The sender has their own background, knowledge, motivation, emotional state, culture, and understanding of the situation. Meanwhile, the receiver brings an entirely different set of perspectives, which rarely align completely. The sender may believe a message is perfectly clear because, in their mind, ten underlying assumptions need no explanation. However, the receiver cannot automatically know those unstated assumptions. A word that sounds completely neutral to one person may carry strong emotional weight for another. Humor can be interpreted as playful or as disrespect. Similarly, silence might signal agreement, hesitation, uncertainty, or rejection. Communication technology, as a medium, has been most successful in solving is physical separation. Reducing physical distance For most of human history, physical distance was the enemy of communication. The speed of a message depended on how fast a person could travel, how fast a horse could run, how fast a ship could sail, or how quickly a document could be delivered. Modern communication technologies gradually removed this barrier. The telegraph allowed information to cross long distances through electricity for the first time. The telephone allowed human voices to cross distance in real time. Later, computer networks such as ARPANET connected people, machines, and information systems on a larger scale. The World Wide Web then made information stored in different computers and institutions easier to connect and share. After that, email, mobile phones, social media, instant messaging, and videoconferencing made communication faster, cheaper, and more widely available. Today, people across several continents can work together, attend meetings, exchange information, and even maintain long-term relationships, while the delay may be only one or two seconds. From this point of view, communication technology has been very successful in reducing physical distance. But one problem has never been fully solved. Distance has been reduced, but misunderstanding has not disappeared. The reason is not difficult to understand: the most difficult barrier in communication has never been only the…

articles.title: How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026
articles.content: The Amazon Quick User Group – United Kingdom is a community of Amazon Quick users in the United Kingdom who meet quarterly to exchange knowledge, share best practices, learn through hands-on sessions, and discuss their experiences using the service. These user groups function as collaborative forums where members learn, connect, and innovate together. Whether you’re already using Amazon Quick or just getting started, we’d love for you to join the UK Amazon Quick User Group and become part of a growing community that’s redefining how organizations make decisions with data. In this post, we’re thrilled to share our 2026 yearly roundup, highlighting all three quarterly meetups that have taken place since the group’s launch and the momentum that has followed. The events drew more than 150 attendees, and the energy in the room, fueled by agentic AI and the potential of Amazon Quick, was clear. Across industries, customers are using Amazon Quick to turn data chaos into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth. Their work spans real-time incident management, eliminating dashboard sprawl with governed data layers, and automating most support workflows with AI. Why Amazon Quick user groups matter The UK Amazon Quick User Group is a local community of Amazon Quick users who come together quarterly to share knowledge, best practices, and experiences with the service. Amazon Quick user groups serve as collaborative forums where members can: Learn and share – Exchange real-world insights about the capabilities of Amazon Quick, from interactive dashboards and data storytelling to agentic AI-powered automations and custom agents. Members share what works, what doesn’t, and new approaches that drive results. Network – Connect with regional professionals who are solving similar use cases with Amazon Quick for enterprise AI applications, data analytics, and workplace productivity. Problem-solve – Tackle challenges collaboratively by discussing solutions and use cases across different industries and business contexts. Stay updated – Get firsthand knowledge about new features, updates, and emerging best practices directly from peers and experts. Build community – Foster a local support network that complements the broader Amazon Quick community, with trusted contacts who understand UK market and business context. Event overview Over three quarterly meetups this year, the UK community spent real time with Amazon Quick. Not slide decks about it, actual time building with it. People created Amazon Quick custom chat agents for their teams without writing code. They tried Amazon Quick Desktop running on their own laptops, connected to local files and using a connector to access Outlook. They also used Amazon Quick Apps to turn a plain-language description into a working web application. The workshops had attendees automating processes with Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate , while Amazon Quick Research showed how it significantly cuts down the time spent on research. The Amazon Quick chat agent tied it together, an assistant that connects to tools, data and takes actions on your behalf. Every quarter, the sessions got more practical and the questions from the room got sharper. What a typical event looks like All three events were held at the Amazon UK Corporate Office in Shoreditch, London. By 9:45 AM, the room is already buzzing. People reconnect over coffee, swap updates from the last quarter, and newcomers get pulled into conversations before the day even officially begins. From there, the energy carries through the full agenda: customers share real stories about what they’ve built with Amazon Quick, product leads walk through the latest updates, and panels spark the kind of back-and-forth you don’t get from a webinar. The 75-minute hands-on workshop is where it really comes alive, with attendees rolling up their sleeves in provisioned sandbox accounts and experimenting together. By the time we close with a feedback…

articles.title: Pentagon IG refuses to investigate Starlink/Starshield slowdown in Ukraine
articles.content: The Pentagon inspector general's office declined a request from US senators to investigate restrictions recently imposed on the Ukraine military's use of SpaceX's satellite network. Ukraine, which uses SpaceX's Starlink service and the military version known as Starshield, said earlier this month that military drones lost satellite connectivity when traveling above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour). The limit was removed after about 10 days. Five Democratic and four Republican senators sent an October 15 letter to Department of Defense Inspector General Platte Moring, asking for a probe into the reported disruptions of Starlink and Starshield. The letter asked, among other things, "whether any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield services were directed, authorized, or implemented by SpaceX, the Department of Defense, or other US government entities; whether such restrictions were consistent with applicable US government contracts, and what actions, if any, the Department of Defense took in response." articles.title: Here's a Hands-On Look at HomePod Mini 2's New Two-Tone Colors
articles.content: The HomePod mini 2 is launching tomorrow (or in a few hours in Australia and New Zealand) and a new hands-on video from Craig's Tech Talk gives a clear look at the two-tone color design Apple added with some of the color options. For the pink, blue, and green HomePod mini models, the two layers of acoustic fabric are different colors. In pink, the outer layer is a light pink and the inner fabric is more of a coral. For the blue ‌HomePod mini 2‌, the mesh is blue and the fabric underneath is green. The green ‌HomePod mini 2‌ has the green color outside and blue underneath, so it's the opposite of the blue model. You can get a close-up look at the colors at the one-minute mark in the video. The midnight and white ‌HomePod mini 2‌ options also have a bit of a two-tone look, but it is more subtle than the pink, blue, and green models. Apple's original ‌HomePod‌ mini also used a mesh fabric, but it did not have a two-tone color look. articles.title: Howler will have AI answer your questions, then burn the chat
articles.content: If you want to ask AI a question and watch the conversation go up in virtual flames when you're done, there's a new Mac app for that. Howler is an open-source app from a Chinese developer going by Aries Zhou, and it takes incognito mode AI questions to a new level by making them graphically interesting and easy to access right from the desktop of a macOS device. Anyone familiar with the Harry Potter series is likely to know where the name comes from - Howlers are letters that scream in recipients’ faces and then burst into flames, destroying themselves, which is the exact same thing the prompts ostensibly do once a user taps the Escape key. The Howler app displays a parchment-esque letter on the screen whenever the user presses Option+H, complete with a little wax seal that shows a letter representing their chosen model. Responses to queries are written out “at a hand’s pace,” per Howler’s website, first in glowing gold that settles to a sepia-toned print. “Besides needing translation at any time, I often want to look up a concept or learn about an event on the fly, without wanting to switch to a browser or open a separate session in Chat,” Zhou wrote in a comment on his Hacker News post showing off the applet. “So I made Howler, dedicated to Harry Potter fans, always there when you call, burning after reading.” The biggest catch to using Howler is that setting it up involves either using an AI service that can run commands, like Claude Code or another coding agent, or running the configuration commands manually. The recommended method involves pasting a setup prompt into the agent's input field. Once set up, Howler can connect to supported AI models using an API key, or to compatible models running locally. Howler’s website states that the API key never enters the chat and is stored in the macOS Keychain for safety. In addition to the API key for the chosen model staying local and not being printed, Howler is described on its website as only storing messages in memory with no history, sending requests straight to the chosen AI service and never through a relay, keeping no logs, and only connecting to an outside service to check for updates - and even that feature can be disabled. It’s a handy tool for those who want to ask AI questions without leaving a chat history on their Mac – like trying to remember the name of that damn function you’re supposed to have down by now, or whether Memorial Day or Labor Day is the one in the fall. Just don’t assume the AI provider won’t retain a record of the exchange. “Unlike regular conversations, it doesn't take up your conversation list, and you don't have to think about cleaning it up or archiving it afterward,” Zhou explained. “It's only for handling your sudden flashes of inspiration or a moment of confusion.” And it does it with panache - sure, it’s just an interface for an AI model one could find elsewhere, but it’s easily conjured, dismissed with a snap, and is open source, to boot. You can find Howler on GitHub, or download it from its website, both linked above. ®
articles.author: Brandon Vigliarolo

articles.title: Nvidia Chief Seen As Target of Chinese Spy Plot
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence. A top executive at a Singapore-based data center company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China. And now American officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset (source paywalled; alternative source), funneling information to Beijing. But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive. For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in artificial intelligence. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump's, set off alarms at the White House. Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia's chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China. This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts. American officials already suspected that Ms. Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced A.I. chips. But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities, including that Mr. Huang had insights into Mr. Trump's thinking on an issue of vital importance to both nations, one likely to come up when the president visits China next month. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the United States has maintained in developing cutting-edge A.I. models. The surveillance of Ms. Huang continues, they said, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips. Nvidia said in a statement: "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." Nvidia is "confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." Customers like Megaspeed, the company that employed Ms. Huang, "receive ordinary business information -- not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets -- and zero information relevant to national security," the company added. In a statement to The New York Times, Megaspeed said that its "current leadership" takes the matter "extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations." It added that "outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the U.S. government that we are fully committed to cooperating." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
