articles.title: Startup wants to make AI agents safe for DevOps duty
articles.content: Vera Platforms, a startup founded by researchers at the University of Michigan, believes there's a way to make agents trustworthy enough to handle DevOps. DevOps, which focuses on how software gets deployed and operated, is a particularly unforgiving affair. While AI agents have some leeway to make mistakes and correct errors as they generate code and work through a prompt, it's an entirely different matter when they make changes to real infrastructure running production workloads. "Live infrastructure is unforgiving," Ang Chen, CEO of Vera Platforms and an associate professor at the University of Michigan, told The Register . "An incorrect change can take down a service, open a security hole or erase data. Mistakes are often irreversible, and there’s no safe way to experiment: running code against production infra just to see what happens isn’t an option." For the past few years, Chen and his colleagues have been working on a way to benchmark agentic DevOps and a gym – a simulation environment – to help AI models get better at DevOps tasks. "From the research that we did, we've figured out various weaknesses of leading models," said Chen. "For instance, [Anthropic's] Claude, although it's very strong with Python generation, it just has some fundamental limitations that it can't get right when it comes to DevOps." An example of that, Chen said, is that when they asked Claude or OpenAI's Codex to decommission resources in the AWS cloud, the models didn't look beyond the default region. "The default region is us-east-1," he explained. "There are various regions in AWS, but Claude doesn't have this awareness that the cloud resources could exist in multiple regions, so it only decommissioned part of the resource." The fundamental reason, he said, is that these models have seen a lot of public code, but a lot less operational tracing. Vera Platforms aims to remedy the situation with three products: vera-gym, a playground environment that emulates production infrastructure; vera-bench, a test for measuring where AI agents fumble DevOps tasks; and vera-agents, AI agents that have been trained in vera-gym and are ready to be deployed for DevOps tasks. The CloudOpsBench test being released builds upon work done in 2024 that was presented at NeurIPS. According to Chen, Claude and Codex only score about a 50 percent pass rate. "It's a very, very hard set of tasks," he said. The test covers tasks like deleting decommissioned S3 buckets , repairing a compliance event pipeline , and restoring DynamoDB write autoscaling . "The tasks are authored by senior infra operators with many years of experience, with rigorous peer review," said Chen. This benchmark has the advantage of not requiring an actual cloud deployment. "We have a high fidelity simulator that mimics Amazon behavior," said Chen. "So the rollout, the performance of the agent on the real cloud and the performance of the agent in our emulator is exactly the same. So for every API, we have this comparison and the agent sees the same thing." Vera-agents, Chen said, should be available in Q1 2027. In their academic work, the researchers describe cloud infrastructure as "critical but tedious work." With a bit more training, maybe AI agents can take over and keep things boring. ®

articles.title: Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream
articles.content: This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies . For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules? It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user. These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want? A Personal AI report , commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor. Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction. With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report. The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit. The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users: True wireless earbuds – 3 hours Wireless headphones – 3 hours Smart glasses – 5 hours Audio glasses – 6 hours Smartwatches – 9 hours Smart rings, necklaces and pendants – 8 hours Consumers want AI that is personal and understands their context — they’re looking for smooth, intuitive experiences that are marked by privacy, security, and user control. articles.title: Trump declares robot imports a national security threat
articles.content: President Donald Trump has declared the imports of foreign-made factory robots to be a national security threat—ordering new US negotiations with trading partners while holding out the possibility of imposing new tariffs on such robot imports in the future. Issued on October 28, Trump’s presidential proclamation represents heightened government scrutiny of foreign-made industrial robots that could complicate the manufacturing operations of major US corporations that rely on such robots. Those companies include Detroit automakers General Motors and Ford, electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla , and aerospace and defense giants like Boeing and Lockheed Martin. Trump’s proclamation describes industrial robots and machinery as being crucial for producing US military weapon systems along with representing a “driving force” behind all critical infrastructure sectors within the US economy. The proclamation cites an investigation under US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick as having found that US imports of such robots “pose[] risks to the United States industrial base and threatens the long-term competitiveness of the United States in a sector that is increasingly vital to national security.” Read full article Comments
articles.author: Jeremy Hsu

articles.title: Apple Lowers App Store Fees in Taiwan Starting October 31
articles.content: Apple is lowering the commission that it collects in Taiwan to 26 percent, down from 30 percent. Apple plans to drop the rate for in-app purchase and paid app transactions on the iOS and iPadOS Taiwan storefront starting on October 31. The commission update comes after Apple held discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission (TFTC). In a statement to MacRumors , Apple said the fee reduction reflects its ongoing commitment to developers. We're making updates to the Taiwan storefront of the App Store following constructive discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission. These changes reflect our ongoing commitment to providing developers with a thriving marketplace and ensuring the App Store remains the safest, most trusted platform for users. We will continue to equip developers with the tools, resources, and support they need to build, grow, and scale successful businesses on the App Store. Apple previously adopted the 26 percent commission rate in Japan and the European Union . Apple also negotiated a 25 percent commission in China after discussions with China's State Administration for Market Regulation. Apple normally charges a lower rate for Small Business Program members, but the announcement about the Taiwan commission changes doesn't include that information. articles.title: Alphabet Heads For a $500 Billion Drop In Market Value
articles.content: Yesterday, Google reported its Q3 results that showed searches made through its AI Mode generate less revenue than traditional search, even as overall search revenue grew 12% year over year to $63.25 billion. The news sent Alphabet shares plunging, with Bespoke Investment Group reporting that the stock is on track for its steepest post-earnings decline since the company went public in 2004. Yahoo Finance reports: At its low, Alphabet had lost $524 billion in stock market value, the second-biggest one-day loss ever for a US-listed company. Only Nvidia has lost more, about $593 billion on Jan. 27, 2025, the day China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors. Alphabet would need to close at about $274.75, down roughly 15%, to take Nvidia's record, by Yahoo Finance calculations. It has already blown past the $400 billion SpaceX lost on June 22, the previous No. 2. In dollars, it's Alphabet's worst day by far. Its previous worst was about $275 billion on July 23. It's also on track for the stock's steepest drop after an earnings report since the company went public, according to Bespoke Investment Group. The previous low was a slide of nearly 10% in July 2008. [...] US-listed stocks have shed $200 billion or more in a single session 18 times this year through Wednesday. That's up from 13 in all of 2025 and none before 2022, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bloomberg data. Alphabet alone has lost about $1.4 trillion since its record in May. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Trump ignored intel on China’s Nvidia spy to protect company’s stock, report says
articles.content: Donald Trump apparently is so aligned with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—who has become the president’s key advisor on AI —that he ignored intelligence indicating that Huang was the target of a “Chinese spy plot,” and did so partly to protect Nvidia’s stock. The New York Times spoke with people briefed on US intelligence agencies’ surveillance and granted them anonymity to discuss findings drawn from “classified intelligence.” According to sources, about a year ago, Trump was briefed that “Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access” to Huang. That “someone” was Alice Huang, or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen and former top executive at a Singapore cloud company called Megaspeed. According to sources, the US had already suspected that Alice Huang—who is not related to Jensen Huang—was helping China evade export controls to gain access to high-end Nvidia chips through Megaspeed. But it alarmed investigators to discover that she may have used her role at Megaspeed to gain direct access to Jensen Huang. It’s now believed she may have leveraged that closeness to feed China intel not only on one of America’s leading AI companies, but also to influence Trump’s thinking on AI. As Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent noted last month ahead of Trump’s AI talks with China President Xi Jinping, “the president is completely aligned with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia.” Read full article Comments

articles.title: Prime Intellect Releases Prime Mega MoE: Trainable Fused MoE Kernel, 3.11x Faster Forward Pass
articles.content: Prime Intellect has released Prime Mega MoE , a training extension of DeepSeek’s fused Mega MoE kernel. DeepSeek’s kernel only ran the forward pass. Prime Intellect added a fast, overlapping backward pass. That makes the fused kernel usable for training, not just inference. In its prime-rl trainer, full training steps on Qwen3 MoE models run up to 34% faster. Against TorchTitan, the gain reaches 55%. For teams training mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, that is a direct cut in GPU hours. TL;DR Size: A GPU kernel, not a model. Tested on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-235B-A22B (128 experts, top-8 routing). Runs on: NVIDIA Hopper (blockwise FP8) and Blackwell (MXFP8) GPUs, BF16 on both. Published numbers use 8×H200 nodes, 32 to 128 GPUs. Performance: 32% to 34% faster full training steps than the prime-rl baseline. 48% to 55% faster than TorchTitan. Best: 3.11x faster forward pass on a Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE layer (12.0 ms to 3.9 ms). Worst: 1.24x backward pass on a Qwen3-235B-A22B MoE layer (30.5 ms to 24.6 ms). What is Prime Mega MoE? Prime Mega MoE is a fused, overlapping MoE kernel for training from Prime Intellect. It builds on the Mega MoE kernel in DeepSeek’s open-source DeepGEMM library. Why is MoE training communication-bound? In an MoE model, each token goes to a small subset of experts. Those experts sit on different GPUs. So every layer sends tokens out, runs expert math, and sends results back. This happens in the forward pass and again in the backward pass. In a standard setup, these are separate operations. The GPU sorts tokens and waits on the transport layer. Then it computes, hands results back, and waits again. Those waits are idle GPU time. How does the fused kernel work? DeepSeek’s Mega MoE , added to DeepGEMM in April 2026, replaces that chain with one kernel call. It fuses expert-parallel dispatch, the 2 expert linear layers, SwiGLU, and combine. While one token group is in transit, the kernel computes on a group that already arrived. It also skips intermediate tensors by using GPU-only scratch buffers. But it only shipped a forward implementation. Prime Intellect wrote the missing backward kernel, also overlapping. Supported types are BF16, MXFP8 (Blackwell only) and blockwise FP8 (Hopper only). The prime-rl config also exposes an fp8_bwd mode: BF16 forward, FP8 backward. How fast is Prime Mega MoE? All numbers below are self-reported by Prime Intellect. Training steps use 8×H200 nodes, FP8, 16,384-token sequences and full activation checkpointing. Each result is the mean of steps 6 to 20. Full training step, seconds (lower is better): Model (cluster) prime-rl baseline TorchTitan (FP8) Prime Mega MoE Gain vs baseline Gain vs TorchTitan Qwen3-30B-A3B (32 H200) 2.78 3.07 2.08 34% 48% Qwen3-235B-A22B (128 H200) 12.72 14.98 9.65 32% 55% Against TorchTitan, throughput rose from 5,337 to 7,886 tokens/s/GPU on the 30B model. On the 235B model, it rose from 1,094 to 1,697. The prime-rl baseline uses torch all-to-all plus DeepGEMM FP8 experts. Single MoE layer, milliseconds (1 node, 8×H200, EP=8, 128 experts, top-8, random routing): Layer Forward Backward Full layer (2x fwd + bwd) Qwen3-30B-A3B 12.0 to 3.9 (3.11x) 15.4 to 8.2 (1.87x) 39.3 to 15.9 (2.47x) Qwen3-235B-A22B 20.7 to 9.5 (2.17x) 30.5 to 24.6 (1.24x) 71.9 to 43.7 (1.64x) The pattern is clear. Forward gains are large, and backward gains are smaller. The headline “up to 3.11x” refers to the forward pass only. How does it compare with other fused MoE options? articles.title: Building intent-driven UI testing with Amazon Nova Act
articles.content: To scale intent-driven UI testing across its product teams, Epsilon , a data, technology, and marketing-services company and part of Publicis Groupe , turned to Amazon Nova Act . With hundreds of millions of consumer profiles and thousands of brand relationships, Epsilon needed UI testing that could keep pace with rapid application changes. The solution could not create maintenance overhead for every product team. Within Epsilon, the Agentic Platform team (50 engineers) builds shared infrastructure so other product teams can build, deploy, govern, and run AI agents safely. With this shared platform, teams get a skills-based agent builder. They also get federated identity and pre-flight authorization, Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, and cross-account provisioning. When a product team wants to adopt AI tooling, they get capabilities without additional configuration and without re-solving identity, security, browser infrastructure, or model integration on their own. One of those managed capabilities is UI testing . With Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Epsilon’s platform team could deliver resilient, intent-driven testing as a service to teams on the platform. In this post, we walk through Epsilon’s architecture for delivering UI testing as a managed platform service, show the core Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration code, highlight a concrete 18-step test workflow, and share best practices and measured results. The challenge: Enhancing coverage, not replacing what works Epsilon’s existing UI testing practice was not broken. The team maintained a Playwright-based regression suite that validated functionality across their web applications, and it worked well. Playwright remains their regression backbone today. The opportunity Epsilon identified was additive, not corrective: Scripted Playwright tests are effective for deterministic regression checks. However, they are tightly coupled to selectors and page structure. Cosmetic UI changes can break them even when the underlying functionality is sound. Multiple product teams needed full testing coverage against their own applications. Standing up browser infrastructure, managing dependencies, and integrating with identity systems per team created duplicative effort. The platform team wanted UI testing to be a managed capability that fit their existing agent model, not a custom CLI that every onboarded team had to operate. The goal: layer intent-based testing on top of the existing Playwright regression suite. Deliver it as a multi-tenant platform service so that each Epsilon product team could consume through the same API surface they used for every other agent capability. Why Epsilon chose Amazon Nova Act and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool Epsilon evaluated options against two requirements: natural-language test authoring (to complement selector-based Playwright tests) and managed browser infrastructure (to fit their multi-tenant platform model). With Amazon Nova Act combined with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, Epsilon could address both. Natural-language steps. Test steps are plain-English instructions executed by Nova Act. They are resilient to cosmetic UI changes and readable by non-engineers. A step like “Confirm the rewards balance is visible” ages far better than a brittle CSS selector. AWS managed, ephemeral browser sessions. With Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, teams get isolated browser instances with no binaries to ship and no display server to maintain. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool also offers live view for human observation or takeover (useful for CAPTCHAs or multi-factor authentication), session recording to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and AWS CloudTrail audit, all without additional configuration. articles.title: Cloud vs. Compliance: Resolving the Tug of War over Data Residency
articles.content: It is a Gold Standard for customers to know that their Data is in safe hands, but at the same time promise of cloud computing was internet without borders, frictionless, global channel where data flowed seamlessly. This article is based on the experience with working for Cloud Platforms that provide services around the globe. The article focuses to explain that when clients sign the Standard Contractual Clauses with the cloud platform providers, it does not automatically guarantee the data will not cross borders even when the data is stored locally in their region. This is because the Cloud Platforms are dynamic in nature as they take automated backups, integrate with other systems to automate processes. To ensure data privacy it is necessary to use hardware security solutions in the server to ensure no data leaks as well as no entry from back door to the servers. There have been many cases reported for cross border data transfers. For Technical Architects of a Cloud platform, Data safeguarding is one of the key challenges of their day-to-day work. With the increase in the number of cases of identity thefts, every region’s government has to implement regulatory framework to safeguard their citizen’s data. It is very important to understand the difference between Data residency and genuine digital sovereignty. While Data residency is more about the geography where data will be stored or where the castle of data will be built, genuine digital sovereignty speaks more about who has the key to that castle! Deconstructing the Stack: Residency vs. Sovereignty Before we analyze how modern architectures adapt, we must first distinctly understand the two terms that are frequently confused as inter related: Data Residency: It specifies the physical, geographic location where data will be stored or at rest, processed or backed up. Achieving residency is the first challenge of deciding the physical infrastructure as data residency is a geographic constraint. The physical infrastructure challenge is resolved by building or leasing localized data centers. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] Data Sovereignty : In simple terms this is a jurisdictional constraint. It dictates that an organization’s data, metadata, custom code and operational workflows remain governed exclusively by laws of the country data resides in. The data is insulated from foreign extraterritorial access laws (for example the US CLOUD ACT) [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] Data residency may ensure safety when data is at rest, but what happens to data in transit? This question is answered by understanding the below layers that constitute towards true digital sovereignty, further the pyramid image explains the significance of each layer [a][b][c] : 1. Data Residency – The physical location of the data center where data will reside. This makes the base of the pyramid 2. Access control (Operational Sovereignty): It means administrative and support activities must be done by trust worthy personnel in the country of Data residency 3. Encryption control (Technical Sovereignty): This means that the client holds the key to the encrypted data and hence the service provider cannot fiddle with something they cannot see! 4. Legal control of Data (Data Sovereignty) : If the software company is headquartered in U.S but stores data in South Africa (that means Data residency is local to South Africa but cloud company is headquartered in U.S) then by lay U.S government can ask provider to hand over the data. Below are few of the major challenges with achieving Digital sovereignty: Every innovation is always posed with challenges as detailed and explained in depth in this article [1] 1. Complex regulations – The regulations change by region 2. Innovations in Technology – We are in the era of AI which changes the equation 3. Frequently changing Customer expectations – Data privacy is the major concern for all customers 4. Threats to Data security – Hackers are also becoming creative so it is necessary to upkeep the data…

articles.title: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro
articles.content: When your team moves a mature PHP application to Java, you gain stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling. A PHP codebase built over the years with Laravel, Symfony, or Doctrine carries business rules in places that are not obvious, from Eloquent traits to XML mapping files, so a structurally similar Java port can compile cleanly and still behave differently. This post shows how to turn PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process using Kiro . Kiro is an AI integrated development environment (IDE) that pairs an AI agent with your codebase to run multi-step engineering tasks with you in the loop. The approach centers on a reusable engine: a shared methodology, a mechanical discovery scanner, and an eight-phase workflow. This engine treats the original PHP application as the specification and refuses to declare the Java port correct until a parity harness verifies it. Prerequisites Before getting started, you need: Familiarity with PHP (Laravel/Eloquent or Symfony/Doctrine). Java knowledge (Spring Boot, JPA) helps you review the generated output, but the engine produces idiomatic Java for you, so you don’t need to rewrite the application in Java yourself. A Kiro workspace with access to Skills and Steering files. PHP 8.0 or newer on the machine running the discovery scanner, and Java 21 with Maven for the generated Spring Boot projects. A basic understanding of migration planning (discovery, translation, and validation). What you will learn in this post You start with an open repository, so you can run the engine yourself rather than read about it. Everything the engine knows lives in a small set of skill files, and with those files, you can run the same methodology in more than one way. Two ways to run the engine: Kiro and AWS Transform Everything here is packaged as skill files: versioned Markdown capability packages that encode the migration methodology (php-to-java-migration) and the discovery scanner workflow (php-model-discovery). Because that knowledge lives in files rather than any one tool, you can run the same methodology in two ways. Method 1: Kiro, interactive and developer-in-the-loop Kiro brings an AI agent into your editor to drive a migration step by step. Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate a PHP application. Kiro then walks the eight-phase workflow with explicit approval gates, so you review the discovery manifest, approve the rulebook, and sign off on each phase before the next begins. It’s the mode used for every example in this post. Method 2: AWS Transform, agentic and at portfolio scale AWS Transform is the AWS agentic AI service for large-scale migration and modernization, and it now integrates natively with Kiro. Through that integration, you can hand AWS Transform the same skill files that govern an interactive Kiro session, so discovery before translation, the parity harness as referee, and ‘ fix the loop, not the code ’ apply to an autonomous run. When each path fits Control and autonomy: Use Kiro to work through the code first: run the skill on one application, read the generated Java, and run the tests. When you want to migrate more, AWS Transform runs the same methodology agentically with review at the checkpoints the skill defines. Scale and novelty: Kiro handles one application at a time and suits first-of-a-kind frameworks. AWS Transform runs many applications as parallel jobs. A shared feedback loop: Both paths read the same skill files, so every rulebook fix made in Kiro improves the next AWS Transform run, and vice versa. Solution overview: One shared brain, many projects The engine is organized around a single principle: one shared brain, many projects. articles.title: REPL While It Works: Inspect a Running Python Program Without Pausing It
articles.content: Usually, without interrupting it, you cannot interactively debug, call functions in, or change the values of variables in a running python program. This article’s technique removes the limitation. There are plenty of python examples showing how an executing script can interrupt its execution to present a console, where you can interact, and then resume execution. Here, the console is your choice of the Python interactive shell prompt, with its Read-Eval-Print Loop (aka REPL), or alternatively, the python PDB debugger. I wanted to do that interacting, but without the interrupting and the resuming parts. While the long running execution continues to run, and without interrupting the program’s flow, I wanted to be able to access objects and invoke other functions concurrently. In the Snow White films, there is a song "Whistle While You Work." (Watch the 1937 version or 2025 version ). I wanted to "REPL While It Works." Audience : The audience for this technique is writers of programs that they use for themselves. Normally, a program’s data and functions, their names, semantics, and usage, are not known by others. Achieving this objective is not hard. The main features of the solution are: A convenient repository for pseudo-global objects which can be created, set, and used both by the threads and by you while in the REPL or PDB. Avoid having to use the global keyword. The application’s real work happens in a started thread or threads. The main thread, after any initiation and starting the threads, drops into REPL, or PDB, or both, one after the other. More details: 1. The repository Create a function to hold the pseudoglobal objects as attributes. Add, change, and use them from anywhere. Avoid having to use the global keyword. def g(): # This function is never called. # It just holds attributes which can be added, set and used from anywhere. pass # example attributes g.d = defaultdict(list) g.finishedthreads=0 g.startedat=time.time() The application functions, are (a) first defined, and then (b) some of them are started as threads. These do the application’s work. See the details in the full program’s code below. Drop into the interactive REPL ro PDB console, or one after the other. #This goes at the bottom of the script while True: # Drop into the PDB console print(f'\n Type os._exit() to terminate the process abruptly, without flushing file buffers, running finally blocks, or executing atexit cleanups.') print(f'\n Type sys.exit(0) to terminate the main and daemon threads. It first raises a SystemExit exception in each thread. This is the full program, including the features above. #!/usr/bin/python3 # run multithreaded tasks, with a repl while they run import code import time from collections import defaultdict import threading import os import sys # 1 Create the repository def g(): # This function is never called. articles.title: Turning a solar power system into its own backup
articles.content: Rather than directly converting photons into electricity, concentrated solar energy uses mirrors to turn sunlight into heat, which can then be used to drive traditional generating turbines. Up to about a decade ago, there was a case to be made that concentrated solar energy had a bright future, as improvements in heat storage had turned it into a way to generate power around the clock. It wasn't to be. While concentrated solar costs fell enough to compete with nuclear power, the price of photovoltaics plunged, making solar panels the cheapest source of power in most locations. Currently, if you have a good site to generate solar power, then the economics of PV panels are hard to beat. That has left us needing to build a mixture of other facilities—typically batteries and natural gas facilities—to handle overnight needs or weather-driven shortfalls. But a small company is promising that it can help avoid the need to build a separate facility. Its version of concentrated solar is designed so that a fossil-fueled backup system shares most of the generating hardware with the solar side. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Canada to Join EU Network of Supercomputers
articles.content: Canada is joining the European Union's supercomputing network to give Canadian companies, startups, and researchers access to European computing resources for AI development. The partnership aims to strengthen AI cooperation and reduce dependence on US technology. Politico reports: The EU's supercomputing network is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, an EU public-private vehicle with an 8.2 billion-euro budget. The network consists of 14 supercomputers (some ranked in the global top 10), 19 AI-focused AI factories and 10 quantum computers. The vehicle will also run seven massive AI data center hubs, known as AI gigafactories, set to be built next year with a total investment cost of 30 billion euros. Experts praised a possible EU-Canadian compute power team-up, but warned it's only the start. "Compute cooperation is one of the most obvious short-term 'middle power' cooperation plays in AI," said Anton Leicht, technology and international affairs fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. But he added that for now "it doesn't put a dent into the actual dependence" on the U.S. "As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn't result in massive buildouts will help," he said. Canada's engagement in the EU's supercomputer network builds further on Canada's previous partial involvement in the EU's flagship research and development program, Horizon Europe. Horizon Europe partially funds EuroHPC. To date, 38 countries have participated in the EU's supercomputing network: 27 EU member countries plus non-EU countries including Norway, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Israel and Turkey. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Old 'Popcorn Time' App Left Hundreds of Thousands of Macs at Risk
articles.content: If you installed Popcorn Time on a Mac years ago, part of the app may still be running, and it may have left your Mac open to attack. Security firm Eye Research has detailed how Time4Popcorn – an unofficial version of the once-popular movie streaming app – left behind a small update checker that scanned for updates every time the Mac started, even for people who hadn't opened the app in years. The checker basically trusted whatever it downloaded, and gave it full permission to change anything on the Mac. What's worse is that Time4Popcorn's developers long abandoned the project, so the website addresses the helper contacted were expiring. That meant anyone who took over one of the addresses could use it to install harmful software on affected machines. Fortunately, Eye Research says it found no evidence that criminals had done so. Eye Research said it took control of an abandoned address used by the update checker, and it estimates that 250,000 to 350,000 Macs were affected. With no developer left to issue a fix, the researchers had to use the checker itself to disable it on more than a million Macs and Windows PCs. It then handed the addresses to the Shadowserver Foundation , a nonprofit cybersecurity group. Even so, this fix doesn't address other vulnerabilities in Time4Popcorn, and some updated addresses remain outside the researchers' control. For that reason, if you're still running that version, the researchers' advice is simple: uninstall it. Time4Popcorn was one of several unofficial versions of Popcorn Time, and it was actually distributed under the Popcorn Time name, so users may not know whether the copy they installed is the affected one. For all the details, check out the Eye Research report . articles.title: Lend and borrow resources across teams with AWS Batch’s quota management for SageMaker Training jobs
articles.content: With the launch of AWS Batch support for Amazon SageMaker Training jobs, customers gained a new fully managed way to queue, schedule, and retry machine learning (ML) training workloads without building their own infrastructure. Instead, they use the queuing and scheduling features of AWS Batch. As organizations scale their artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) operations and onboard more teams, coordinating access to shared graphics processing unit (GPU) capacity can introduce additional communication, coordination, and configuration overhead for administrators. This overhead includes setting up separate queues, adjusting capacity limits, and carefully orchestrating the right workloads to get the right resources at the right time. A core value proposition of AWS Batch is helping customers increase utilization of their compute, and as training environments grow, so does the opportunity to do more with existing capacity. Working backward from customers managing multi-team training environments, we heard a consistent request: give us a way to define allocations per team or project, share idle capacity automatically, and run our highest-priority workloads first. This request led us to build quota management , a new scheduling capability for AWS Batch. Administrators can use it to divide compute capacity into quota shares, organized by team, project, or workload. Each quota share uses configurable resource-sharing strategies that maximize GPU utilization while honoring each team’s allocation when it matters most. This post shows how quota management works, including how to configure quota shares with lending and borrowing strategies, set up in-share preemption for priority workloads, and get started using the SageMaker Python SDK. Quota shares and preemption Administrators can allocate and share constrained GPU resources by defining a quota share for separate entities, such as individual teams or projects. Each quota share includes compute quotas (capacity limits) and resource-sharing strategies for idle compute. These strategies determine whether idle compute is reserved until jobs arrive ( RESERVE ), lent to other quota shares that have work available ( LEND ), or both lent when idle and borrowed when the share has work that might benefit ( LEND_AND_BORROW ). A quota share operates as a virtual queue nested hierarchically within an associated job queue. When scheduling jobs for a job queue, AWS Batch prioritizes quota shares that are under their capacity limits as it iterates through the associated quota shares. If jobs arrive in a quota share that has lent out its capacity, AWS Batch performs cross-share preemption. This reclaims resources for the lending quota share, so administrators don’t need to track down the jobs borrowing capacity and terminate them on their own. If jobs arrive in a quota share that is at or above its capacity limit, AWS Batch checks whether there’s available capacity to borrow from another quota share. If so, workloads can run using otherwise-idle capacity. You can turn on priority-based in-share preemption when you configure a quota share. Where cross-share preemption reclaims lent capacity as jobs arrive in a lending quota share, in-share preemption preempts lower priority jobs that are in the SCHEDULED, STARTING, or RUNNING state. This allows higher priority jobs at the front of the queue to start running sooner. Prerequisites Before you proceed with this example, you must have an AWS account with permissions to create and manage AWS Batch resources. For this example, see the sample IAM permissions needed to invoke AWS Batch and SageMaker APIs. The example uses the SageMaker Python SDK v3. articles.title: How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway
articles.content: This post was co-written with Nikhil Kumar and Shakir Khan from MoEngage. When engineering teams start building AI agents, the capabilities those agents need usually already exist as internal APIs. Campaign creation, segment queries, delivery stats. The challenge isn’t building new functionality. The challenge is making hundreds of private APIs safely reachable by agents without exposing them to the public internet, without giving models control over identity, and without flooding context windows with hundreds of tool definitions. MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use to deliver personalized experiences across push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS, faced exactly this problem. Behind the product sit roughly 400 internal REST APIs, built by 25 engineering teams, running in private virtual private clouds (VPCs) across seven AWS Regions. MoEngage isolates these APIs regionally to meet data residency commitments and doesn’t expose them to the public internet. The capability the agents needed was already running in production. Making it reachable, safely, was the hard part. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage used AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to turn those private APIs into permission-scoped agent tools. The approach saved MoEngage an estimated six months of platform engineering effort, and onboarding a new API now takes hours instead of days. No product team wrote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server code, no networking was provisioned per integration, and no public endpoint exists anywhere in the path. Why 20 MCP servers was the wrong answer The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives agents a standard way to discover and call tools. The straightforward path to adopting it is for each team to expose its own MCP server. MoEngage costed that out and rejected it. Over 20 MCP servers means over 20 deployments to monitor, patch, and keep protocol-compatible as MCP evolves. Cross-domain agents, the useful ones that read a campaign, check its segment, and inspect delivery stats, would need to connect to several servers and reconcile them. And every team would need MCP expertise unrelated to its actual product work. So MoEngage established the principle that shaped everything that followed: Individual engineering teams do not implement MCP. Teams build REST APIs and declare which operations should be tools. The AI Platform team owns the MCP layer end to end. A team’s responsibility ends at a well-described OpenAPI spec. That principle immediately created three requirements: a central tool surface that agents connect to once rather than per-service, per-agent authorization enforced server-side rather than by convention, and private connectivity that does not need to be rebuilt for every new API. Building all of this from scratch was an option. A custom central MCP server would solve the 20-servers problem but leave MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, all of it undifferentiated work that does not make MoEngage’s agents smarter or its customers’ campaigns better. Four constraints that shaped the architecture Before evaluating any solution, MoEngage defined four constraints. All four had to be met simultaneously. A solution that addressed two but broke the third and fourth was not viable. Nothing gets a public endpoint. MoEngage’s internal APIs are VPC-private by policy. Any solution that required exposing them, even behind additional authentication, was a non-starter. The conventional workaround is per-integration networking: a NAT gateway here, a reverse proxy there, a VPN tunnel for the third one. Multiply that by seven Regions and the operational surface grows faster than the set of agents does. Every new API would mean another networking change request, another set of security reviews, another piece of infrastructure…

articles.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion, slashing user options
articles.content: DoorDash has announced a deal to buy delivery market competitor Instacart, in a move that will leave users with one fewer iPhone app-based delivery option. DoorDash has confirmed plans to buy Instacart. DoorDash announced the move via a press release , noting that the $65-a-share buyout price represents a 26% premium on Instacart's closing price from October 22, 2026. The aggregate transaction consideration will be made up of at least 75% cash, with shareholders able to choose cash or DoorDash shares as payment. While the deal is yet to be completed, it's in both company's interests for the purchase to go ahead. Termination fees would see Instacart pay $650 million and DoorDash $1.25 billion should the deal falter. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums
articles.author: Oliver Haslam <oliver@monkeymanmedia.com>

articles.title: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it's fixing that with more ads
articles.content: Google parent Alphabet reported its Q3 financial results on Wednesday afternoon, showing a healthy rise in revenue for the months of July to September. But the company's stock price has taken a beating, marking one of the largest post-earnings drops in its history. It comes down to several troubling aspects of the new report, including an admission by the company that AI search isn't earning as much as organic search, and despite that, Google expects to spend even more on AI next year. The company took in almost $128 billion in Q3 2026, earning more than $26 billion in net income. These may sound like good numbers, but financial markets are not impressed. While revenue is up 25 percent versus last year, net income is almost $9 billion lower. As of this story's publication, the stock price is down almost 12 percent, and it was down about 13 percent earlier in the day. While revenue was up 25 percent year over year, analysts expected more. Google reported earnings per share of $2.12, but the consensus projection ahead of Wednesday was $3.02. Google's Cloud products actually beat expectations, crossing $30 billion in revenue. That's about a billion more than analyst guesses. Read full article Comments
articles.author: Ryan Whitwam

articles.title: Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS
articles.content: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL joins the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano , Nano Omni , Super , Ultra , and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning models already available on AWS. It’s a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that activates 12B parameters per token. It combines reasoning and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding, so one model serves both text and visual tasks. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) , Amazon EKS Auto Mode , and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS . About Nemotron 3.5 Super VL NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open multimodal model distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. NVIDIA publishes the weights, training datasets, and post-training recipes, so you can customize the model for domain-specific workloads and run it on infrastructure you control. Model details: 120B total parameters, 12B active per token. Hybrid Mamba-2, MoE , and attention layers with a RADIO vision encoder. Context length up to 1M tokens. Input: text, image, document, and video. Output: text. BF16 and NVFP4 checkpoints. NVIDIA reports 63.44 percent on Hermes Bench and 87.05 percent on LangChain agent evaluations, and 80.8 percent on the CharXiv chart-reasoning benchmark. ( technical report ) Model architecture Nemotron 3.5 Super VL uses a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE architecture, interleaving Mamba-2, attention, and expert layers. Sparse routing activates 12B of the 120B parameters per token, so compute per token matches a much smaller model while GPU memory still holds the full weights. Mamba-2 layers carry a constant-size state during generation, so their memory does not grow with sequence length the way KV cache does, which keeps long contexts affordable. A recursively shared Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head supports native speculative decoding. Use cases Nemotron 3.5 Super VL supports agent workflows that combine reasoning with visual understanding: Coding: test and validate code, analyze errors, recommend fixes. Web research: cross-reference and verify sources returned by search tools. Document intelligence: read tables, charts, and page layouts to produce summaries. Cyber security: identify vulnerabilities and triage threats. Video understanding: search, content, review, and incident analysis. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL integrates with major open agent frameworks and orchestration systems through NVIDIA reference implementations, cookbooks, and the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit . For the full list of supported frameworks, see the NVIDIA developer blog . Minimum GPU configurations vLLM (GPU Model / min count) BF16 NVFP4 B200/GB200 8 2 B300/GB300 4 1 H200 8 4 H100 16 8 Deployment on AWS This section gives an overview of architecture, validation, and performance evaluation approaches. A detailed walkthrough of deploying Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3 Ultra on AWS is available in the aws-do-eks project, including prerequisites, cluster creation, model weights download, deployment, testing, benchmarking, and cleanup. The same pattern can also be applied to other models in the NVIDIA Nemotron family. Deployment architecture The reference implementation runs on standard Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS. With EKS Auto Mode, AWS manages scaling, GPU, and EFA support in the cluster on your behalf. The Kubernetes manifests for model deployment are the same for each of the orchestrator options. Each cluster has a control plane hosting the Kubernetes API and a data plane of CPU and GPU nodes. CPU nodes run system and test pods, while the GPU nodes run the model. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) stores the container images, a shared Amazon FSx for Lustre volume holds the model weights, and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) connects the GPU nodes. articles.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
articles.content: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO is selling investors a story. The numbers tell another one
articles.content: Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Company’s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI . I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy. Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here . And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com , and follow me on X @thesullivan . Anthropic IPO: Do retail investors know what they’re getting into? Anthropic officially filed its IPO papers earlier this week, hoping to raise up to $100 billion, and as much as 20% of the shares may be reserved for retail investors (aka regular folks). On Tuesday, Meta said it would sell equity shares on the public market to raise $95 billion to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. Retail investors have long been exposed to the AI business through shares in tech behemoths like Google and Microsoft, but they’re now getting the chance to place bets on pure-play AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI. Do they know what they’re getting into? I have my doubts. Does anyone really know what we’re getting into? Retail investors make investing decisions differently from institutional investors (such as pension funds or hedge funds). While institutional investors dig into the financials of prospective investments, retail investors often base their decisions on the narrative a company lays out as it goes public. “Retail investors buy the story, not the model,” PitchBook senior late-stage research analyst Harrison Rolfes tells Fast Company . “The story for Anthropic is $11.6 billion of revenue in a single quarter; the model is $8.9 billion spent on compute in six months and more than $430 billion of non-cancelable compute contracts.” The financials in Anthropic’s S-1 imply an 85% gross margin, but Rolfes points out that after factoring in the cost of the compute that trains the next model, only “about 45 cents of each revenue dollar is left.” A big chunk of Anthropic’s commitments—at least $269 billion—is owed to Amazon, Google, and Microsoft for cloud computing resources through 2036. Ten years is a long timeline for a commitment that big, especially when it’s not even clear that AI will continue to be served almost exclusively from cloud servers a decade from now. WebAI’s David Stout argues that as AI becomes more efficient and capable of running directly on devices (see Apple’s new iMac and MacBook Pro with the M6 chip), the industry risks pouring trillions into data centers it may not ultimately need. WebAI is one of a wave of companies building private, localized AI that runs on devices organizations already own. As the cadence of new model releases accelerates, enterprises are struggling to keep up—to build the infrastructure and applications they need to take advantage of the latest models’ capabilities. The pace at which enterprises can adapt their processes and people to AI may be limited by forces outside the AI labs’ control. For example, the best AI model is still only as good as the contextual data an enterprise can give it, and preparing that data and building the conduits to get it to the right place takes time and resources. A lot is riding on how well workers adapt. Workers will need time to build trust in AI to produce accurate outputs and make good decisions. How quickly that happens depends on the specific application, the company’s culture and leadership, and the industry in which it operates. For example, the healthcare industry is inefficient and wasteful and has much to gain from AI, but it’s also notoriously slow to adopt new technologies. The big question is whether enterprises will continue to spend aggressively on AI so that Anthropic can earn enough profit to cover its huge infrastructure commitments. Enterprises will have to keep pushing—and investing—even when they aren’t yet seeing measurable productivity and efficiency gains from AI. None of this is assured, and that’s…

articles.title: Why MCP servers should tell agents what to do next
articles.content: Many MCP servers do one thing. An agent asks for data, and the server hands it back. AWS’s James Ward thinks that leaves a lot on the table. The protocol works best, he told me, when the server acts less like a database and more like another voice in the conversation. Ward is a principal developer advocate at AWS and sits on the technical committee of the Agentic AI Foundation, the Linux Foundation group that now houses MCP. I sat down with him last week at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose the day before he and co-presenter Alexander Ioffe were set to give a session on moving MCP from a basic API to an agent integration interface. “Many times our MCP servers are just these APIs, like ‘get me the customers,’ and that is a good place to start,” Ward said. “I imagine MCP as the third person in this conversation, or a fourth or a fifth, depending on how many MCP servers you have.” In practice, that means a tool response carries guidance with the data. It tells the agent what it just did, what it might want to do next, and where to find more. The other half of his pitch is visibility. Web developers can trace a click on a page all the way down to the database. “MCP by default doesn’t have any way to do trace ID,” Ward said. The workaround AWS uses is rather low-tech. Add a session ID parameter to the tools and tell the agent to pass it on every call, so individual calls can be stitched into one journey. A second parameter can carry the user’s prompt or a summary of their goal. Teams can then compare what the user wanted with the path the agent took, build an eval around it, adjust a tool description or parameter, and measure whether more tasks get completed. Ward said AWS built much of this for the MCP servers its own developers use. In May, AWS opened its MCP Server to everyone and added Lambda diagnostics in September . In an Agentic AI Foundation profile published before the conference, Ward described an agent fetching customer records one at a time because the server only offered a one-record tool. Watching the full journey is how teams spot that pattern and build a batch tool to fix it. Ward didn’t present MCP as the only solution. AWS also ships a CLI and skills, he said, partly because MCP’s OAuth model can’t toggle between AWS user profiles the way the CLI can. Which works best depends on the model, the tool descriptions, and how the agent discovers tools, so AWS tests them against each other with evals. None of this is exotic, and Ward knows it. “There’s nothing new under the sun,” he said. Observe the journey, reproduce it, measure it, and improve it. The difference is that teams now have to understand the path a human and an agent take together, and test whether changes to their tools actually help them finish the task. The post Why MCP servers should tell agents what to do next appeared first on The New Stack .

articles.title: Elon Musk's SpaceX buying out 418 homes near flagship AI data center, but only if they drop participation in lawsuit
articles.content: SpaceXSI, Elon Musk’s data center business powering Grok, is reportedly buying 418 properties in Colonial Hills, Southaven, which sits about half a mile from the powerplant that the company will use to power its data centers in the area. According to The Guardian , real estate agents have been going door to door, offering owners deals on behalf of the company provided that they do not join a class-action lawsuit over the noise pollution coming from the gas turbines that power its GPUs. MZX, the SpaceXSI subsidiary that operates the Colossus II site, circulated an open letter to nearby residents, saying that it “requires property for its business purposes,” with Southaven mayor Darren Musselwhite saying that they will be used to house SpaceXSI staff that the company will need as it expands operations. Musk himself is reportedly staying in the area in an Airstream trailer four nights per week to personally oversee the data center build-out needed to power Grok AI. The bigger issue here, though, is the requirement that sellers must sign an agreement that prevents them from joining the ongoing case against the company for noise pollution. The Colossus 1 and 2 sites have been in hot water since they started operating, primarily for their use of unpermitted turbines and the air pollution that they bring . SpaceXSI has since promised that it will remove all its unpermitted turbines in a year, especially as its 1.2-gigawatt powerplant comes online. However, this apparently hasn’t resolved the noise pollution issue that the community has been complaining about. “It sounds like an airplane engine but it’s continuous, it’s incredibly loud. I’ve been woken up at 2am by it, I’ve been woken up at 3am by it. I sometimes have to just get away from it because it makes me so angry,” piano teacher Elizabeth Rose, who lives a couple of miles from the site, told the publication. One of the plaintiffs in the class-action, Jason Haley, also said to The Guardian , “There’s a high-pitched hum and then another sound like an airplane over your house. It’s been so torturous I can’t sleep; I just leave the house or turn on some music until I fall asleep completely exhausted. It drives you insane. You also lose hope because you’re being ignored or dismissed. There’s no escape.” The company has denied all the allegations against it, saying that it has adjusted its power output and installed sound-dampening walls to reduce the impact on the neighborhood. Musselwhite also said that city monitors have not detected the site breaching the local ordinance limit of 70 decibels, although some experts say that persistent noise as low as 50 decibels could have adverse health impacts. Opposition against the noise pollution and Musk’s purchases aren’t unanimous, though. Some residents aren’t as affected by the noise pollution, while local businesses are experiencing increased activity. Other people have also agreed to sell just so they could get away from the noise. The mayor says that the buyout isn’t intended to turn Colonial Hills into a company town. “The buyout has multiple purposes which are to provide homes for some employees and a goodwill gesture from a good corporate citizen for those who perceive the industrial development near them as negative,” Musselwhite said.

articles.title: Keeping Angular Tabs in Sync with BroadcastChannel and Signals
articles.content: A small example with a shared preference, persistent state, and no message loops. Let’s say our application has a menu with a “Show only pinned items” setting. We open the application in two tabs, change the setting in one, and expect the other to follow. Inside each tab, an Angular service can hold the setting in a signal. But each tab runs its own application and has its own service instance. Changing one signal does not update the other. Let’s connect them with BroadcastChannel and keep the example small: one setting, one service, and one checkbox. The code below targets an existing Angular application with client rendering. It assumes a browser with working BroadcastChannel and localStorage access. Applications with server rendering need a browser-only boundary around this service. What should each part do? We will use localStorage to keep the current preference, BroadcastChannel to tell other tabs that it changed, and a signal to expose the value to Angular templates. The message will contain only the kind of change. When another tab receives it, that tab reads the current value from storage. Why read it again? A message may be handled after another write has already happened. Reading storage avoids replacing the current preference with an older value carried by a delayed notification. BroadcastChannel connects listeners using the same channel name. The sending channel object does not receive its own message, so we must update the originating tab ourselves. This example uses ordinary same-origin tabs in the same browser profile; embedded pages can have additional storage-partition restrictions . Create the service Put the service in src/app/menu-preferences.service.ts: import { DestroyRef, Injectable, inject, signal } from '@angular/core'; const STORAGE_KEY = 'demo:menu:pinned-only'; const CHANNEL_NAME = 'demo:menu-preferences:v1'; type PreferenceChanged = { type: 'pinned-only-changed'; }; function isPreferenceChanged(value: unknown): value is PreferenceChanged { return ( typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && 'type' in value && value.type === 'pinned-only-changed' ); } @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) export class MenuPreferencesService { private readonly channel = new BroadcastChannel(CHANNEL_NAME); private readonly destroyRef = inject(DestroyRef); private readonly pinnedOnlyState = signal(this.readPinnedOnly()); readonly pinnedOnly = this.pinnedOnlyState.asReadonly(); constructor() { this.channel.onmessage = ({ data }: MessageEvent<unknown>) => { if (isPreferenceChanged(data)) { this.refresh(); } }; this.destroyRef.onDestroy(() => this.channel.close()); } setPinnedOnly(value: boolean): void { localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, String(value)); this.refresh(); this.channel.postMessage({ type: 'pinned-only-changed', } satisfies PreferenceChanged); } private refresh(): void { this.pinnedOnlyState.set(this.readPinnedOnly()); } private readPinnedOnly(): boolean { return localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY) === 'true'; } } There are two paths through this service. A local change calls setPinnedOnly(): it saves the preference, refreshes the local signal, and sends a notification. An incoming notification calls refresh(): it only reads storage and updates the signal. That difference prevents a loop. Receiving a message never sends another message, and it never writes an old value back to storage. Keep postMessage() on the local-change path. An effect that broadcasts every signal update would also broadcast changes received from other tabs. The writable signal is private. Components get a read-only view and use setPinnedOnly() to change the setting, so they cannot accidentally skip persistence or notification. DestroyRef closes the channel when the service’s injector is destroyed. Since this service uses providedIn: 'root', its lifetime is tied to the application, not to one checkbox component. articles.title: MentorAgent: Turn Your .NET Methods into AI Actions Under Your Rules
articles.content: MentorAgent is an open-source library for .NET 10 that puts an AI agent between your systems and your users , and keeps it under your rules . On one side, the agent uses what you already have: the methods of your .NET application, the tools of MCP servers, other agents over A2A. On the other side, your agent and its actions reach people and programs wherever they are: on the web, on mobile, in AI assistants, in other agents, in scripts and services. In the middle, MentorAgent enforces your rules, splits work among specialists and teams, knows the user’s page, keeps costs in check, shows what happened and runs the model you choose, in the cloud or local. MentorAgent at a glance Your systems: .NET methods marked with [MentorAction], tools from MCP servers, agents reached over A2A. MentorAgent: six capabilities between the two sides: governance, specialists and teams, pages and skills, cost control, observability, and the model you choose, in the cloud or local. Wherever your users are: web and mobile apps, AI assistants through MCP, other agents through A2A, scripts and services through HTTP and Server-Sent Events. Why MentorAgent A chatbot that answers questions is easy to build. An agent that acts inside a business application is not. As soon as it can change data, the questions change too: What can it use: your services, MCP tools, other agents? Who may ask for what, and who confirms changes? How does it split complex work, and how do you see what it did? Which model answers, and what does it cost? Where do users meet it: web, mobile, an AI assistant, another system? MentorAgent answers each of these in your code, not in the prompt. Your systems: what the agent can use .NET methods The problem. Your services already know how to read an order or issue a refund. Rewriting that logic for an AI framework duplicates it, and the two copies drift apart. What MentorAgent does. You keep your services. A [MentorAction] attribute marks the methods the agent may use, and one call registers the library, the model and the classes to scan: using Microsoft.Extensions.AI; using Novior.MentorAgent.Extensions; using OpenAI; var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args); // Action classes come from the DI container builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderStore, SqlOrderStore>(); builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>(); builder.Services.AddMentorAgent(options => { options.AppName = "ShopFlow back office"; options.ScanAssemblies = [typeof(Program).Assembly]; options.ChatClient = new OpenAIClient(builder.Configuration["OpenAI:Key"]!) .GetChatClient("gpt-4o-mini") .AsIChatClient(); }); builder.Services.AddRazorComponents().AddInteractiveServerComponents(); The result. One source of truth for the business logic. The agent calls the same methods your controllers and pages call. MCP tools and A2A agents The problem. Useful capabilities often live outside your application: a carrier’s tracking service, a warehouse agent, a tool written in another language. What MentorAgent does. Two options connect them. McpServers adds tools from MCP servers, optionally limited to an allow list. RemoteAgents adds A2A agents as specialists the coordinator can hand work to. MCP and A2A have official SDKs for Python, JavaScript and TypeScript, Java, C#, Go and Rust, so those tools and agents can be written in any of them. The result. Your agent works with the rest of your landscape through open standards, not custom integrations. A remote agent runs under its own host’s rules: your roles don’t apply to it, and any user of your agent can reach it. MentorAgent: six capabilities in the middle Governance The problem. “Please ask before refunding” in a prompt is a wish. A model can forget it, misread it, or be talked out of it. What MentorAgent does. The rules live on the method and are enforced every time a tool is called, outside the model: using Novior.MentorAgent.Attributes; public class OrderService(IOrderStore store) { [MentorAction(Description = "Returns the status of…

articles.title: What a 1.0 Can Honestly Promise
articles.content: What turned up when a lease library met a real database, a drifting clock, and a call that never returned This follows a three-part series on checkpointed lease handoff in distributed systems. It stands on its own. The second article in that series taught a distinction the library implemented incorrectly. The distinction is between a clean handoff and a crash. worklease coordinates work between processes with leases: locks that expire unless the holder keeps renewing them. A worker that finishes and releases its lease leaves a checkpoint the next owner can trust. A worker that vanishes leaves one the next owner has to validate. Everything downstream depends on telling them apart: whether to continue or reconcile, and whether the work is available now or only after the lease expires. worklease carried that distinction in a single boolean, and the boolean was wrong in one sequence. Worker A released cleanly. Worker B acquired the lease, started work, and crashed before writing a checkpoint. Worker C acquired it and was told the handoff was clean, because the flag had been inherited from A’s release and only a checkpoint from B would have cleared it. C skipped the validation a crash requires, though B had been working. That isn’t an exotic failure. It is two ordinary events in a row. worklease 1.0 has not been run in production. It has been specified, tested on two backends, and audited, but it has not carried real load. That limits what this article can claim, and the limit is stated in full near the end. Handoff: a flag that described the wrong holder The fix was not a patch to the boolean. The boolean is gone. Every holder now declares how it left: finished, abandoned, or retired. The library infers the one exit no holder can declare, which is that the lease expired with no declaration at all. A successor reads how the previous holder exited, not a flag that might describe someone earlier. The model from the second article held: state is written atomically with the lease renewal, and a fencing counter rejects writes from a holder that has been superseded. What failed was the code around that model. A flag describing the wrong holder was one case. The others were a shutdown path that discarded final state, a renewal loop that trusted a call to return, and a window computed from two clocks. Shutdown: a path the test double forgave Three entry points promised the same thing. Runner.Run, Elect, and pool.Run each documented that the lease was released before they returned. The runner, and the pool through it, also wrote a final checkpoint first. All three did that final work with the caller’s context. On graceful shutdown, that context is already cancelled. On PostgreSQL, both calls failed before reaching the database. The reproduction takes four steps: a work function waits for cancellation, returns its final state along with the context error, the parent context is cancelled, and the next worker tries to acquire. Run returned context canceled. The next Acquire got ErrLeaseHeld until the full TTL elapsed. When it finally acquired, the final state had never been stored, and the handoff looked like a crash. Scaled up, that meant every graceful cancellation of pool.Run discarded each slot's final state and held every lease for a full TTL. The orderly path was the failing one. This was not found by an incident. It was found by reading three docstrings against what the code did, then reproducing the difference on PostgreSQL 16. The reason nothing had caught it is the part worth keeping. The in-memory backend ignored context cancellation, so a cancelled Release simply worked. Every integration spec ran against it. The test double was kinder than the database, and the spec suite was built on the double. The fix has two halves. The first is a cleanup context that survives cancellation of the caller’s, bounded by a timeout: cleanupCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), cleanupTimeout) The second is that the…

articles.title: Robot Picks up Othello
articles.content: Experience is a great teacher. Ask [Jeneus], who, in high school, tried to make a program that played Othello. It didn’t go well. But years later, the idea produced an impressive Othello robot . At first glance, the robot looks a bit like a 3D printer with an aluminum extrusion XYZ motion system. But there’s a lot more to it, not to mention the software to play the game. Check it out in the video below. The Z-axis has a vacuum system that can pick up clear tokens and place them on the board. If you know the game, you might remember that on a real board, players have to flip the tokens as they “capture” pieces. The robot has a smarter way to go. The tokens are clear because they are lit with one of two colors. So flipping the token is a simple LED color change. The LEDs also flash a different color to show you where you can move. The device uses laser-cut components and 3D printed parts in PLA and TPU. Of course, there is a camera for the computer — a Raspberry Pi — to see the board. Overall, a very nicely done project. We’ve seen several checker and chess robots . We wonder if some of them could also play Othello ?
