articles.title: AI demand triggers massive PCB shortage for PC makers as order books full until 2030
articles.content: The AI industry continues to gobble up manufacturing resources that were once dedicated to serving PC, smart device, and gadget makers. We’ve seen huge demand/supply driven price rises in RAM , GPUs, SSDs, and more through 2026. Now that most basic and unglamorous electronics necessity, the PCB, looks set to join them. A news report published by Nikkei Asia quotes several leading PC and PCB industry managers, making it clear we are going to see PCB (and PCB subcomponent) shortages and price rises in the coming months. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI shortages (Image credit: Nvidia) AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supply Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible Chip scarcity assaults auto industry amid the worsening Nexperia and DRAM crisis The custom AI ASIC state of play An unnamed exec from an American PC maker spoke to Nikkei about the dire shortage of PCBs. “Even though PC shipments could decline again next year, we are still struggling to secure enough PCB supplies to meet our needs,” said the manager, who asked to remain anonymous. They were talking about securing enough supplies to make plans for products in the coming year. Several commenters pointed to AI computing demand eating up production capacity. The outlet also talked to business people further up the supply chain – the makers of PCBs and the makers of the components/materials needed to actually make PCBs. Traditional PCB demand is becoming underserved as AI products demand and pay more. One PCB maker talking to Nikkei said that a significant number of products have lead times that have doubled. Specifically, some PCB orders will take as long as 30 months to fulfill. Another PCB supply firm explained to Nikkei that a new order today would not be fulfilled until late in 2028. Though PCB makers are planning to invest and expand, they also need to secure multiple upstream materials. These can include copper clad laminates (CCLs) and the specialized fiberglass used for PCB construction . One Taiwanese PC maker noted that costs for CCLs have surged at least 12 times since July. Moreover, one of the world’s leading suppliers of CCLs has told the Nikkei that it has an order book that is currently filling up to 2030. This situation appears to have occurred despite its plans to triple capacity by 2028. In closely related developments, Nikkei observed that Nvidia recently announced partnerships with several major chip substrate makers. Chip substrates are essentially the tiny and intricate PCBs that CPUs and GPUs are mounted on. Japan's Ibiden, South Korea's Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Unimicron of Taiwan all have new agreements with the Green team. Unimicron is looking at expanding capacity by 2.5x over the next three years. PCBs have been viewed as an unglamorous lower-tech part of the supply chain, partly due to the small numbers on the BoM. That may change. Companies are now racing to ramp up production of advanced PCBs and chip substrates to meet demand, and boost income. Finally, the source report also notes that it is increasingly difficult to get the engineering staff required at new production facilities. Salaries have already risen 20% to 30% across the PCB industry to keep skilled employees.
articles.author: Mark Tyson

articles.title: Coding Dojo co-founder unveils ‘Idea to Launch,’ a 30-day program to help aspiring founders build with AI
articles.content: Richard Wang says he gets inspiration from mentoring aspiring startup founders. (Idea to Launch Photo) Richard Wang , co-founder and former CEO of coding bootcamp Coding Dojo, is launching Idea to Launch , a 30-day program that helps would-be founders turn a startup idea into a working product using AI coding tools and hands-on engineering help. Nearly four years after selling Coding Dojo to Perdoceo for $70 million, Wang was looking for a way to keep doing work that had a measurable impact on people’s lives. He found it in mentoring aspiring founders. Wang thinks AI is about to do for software what smartphones did for video. Cheap cameras and cloud platforms gave rise to the influencer economy, and he believes AI will push the cost of building a product close to zero. “We’re going to create this whole new builder economy that’s about to come in the next three to five years,” he said. “Baby boomers are gifted with cheap housing. I think Gen Z is going to be gifted with a cheap price to build.” He sees plenty of demand. Citing a Shopify-Gallup study and a Zapier/Harris poll, Idea to Launch says 60% of Americans have a business idea but only 9% launch one. Wang said the reasons people hold back include fear of failure, not knowing how to get started, and not wanting to give up a paycheck or benefits. Unlike accelerators such as Techstars or Y Combinator, Idea to Launch doesn’t take equity, and participants don’t have to quit their jobs. Over 10 evening sessions, founders get coaching, run customer interviews, build a product with AI tools such as Lovable, Replit and Cursor, and plan a launch. Each founder also gets 10 hours of one-on-one help from professional engineers. Wang said people without technical backgrounds can now vibe-code 80% to 90% of a product on their own. The hard part, he said, is connecting it to other services, setting up the database correctly and making it secure. “We’ll provide that type of knowledge with real engineering support,” he said. For engineers who have never done customer discovery or marketing, the program fills in the business side. Security researchers have found serious vulnerabilities in apps built on vibe-coding platforms. A 2025 scan found 170 of 1,645 apps built with Lovable exposing user data, and another case this year exposed nearly 19,000 user records. Wang said the program’s engineers will make sure security holes are fixed “before they launch or before they get onto the first customer.” The first cohort starts Jan. 11, followed by three more through April. Each is capped at 15 to 20 founders. Tuition is $3,500 for the inaugural cohort, down from the normal $5,000. Sessions will be held in person in Seattle or Bellevue, and Wang said he expects to pick a space within the next month. He is self-funding the venture. Wang, who immigrated from China at 13 and was the first in his family to attend college, became Coding Dojo’s CEO in 2015. He left in 2017 for Trupanion and returned in 2019. The company grew to $50 million in peak annual revenue, according to Wang, and had 194 employees at the time of the sale, according to GeekWire’s earlier reporting. It operated campuses in several states before shifting online during the pandemic. Wang sees Idea to Launch expanding to other tech hubs, then online, and eventually licensing the program globally, much as Coding Dojo grew to multiple campuses. If the first cohorts go well, he can envision a follow-up program, Launch to Traction, to help founders find more customers. He doesn’t plan to invest in participants’ companies. Having spent years building and selling Coding Dojo, Wang said he knows how hard that road is and would rather “cheer them on from the sidelines.” He said taking VC money at Coding Dojo created pressure to grow 100% a year, something he calls “startup steroids.” For Wang, the point isn’t to find the next unicorn. It’s to give more people a shot at building…

articles.title: Mistral’s Large 4 open weights arrive with a 1-point coding lead over GLM-5.3: “There’s nothing you can’t do with this model that you can do with competitors.”
articles.content: On Thursday, Mistral released the weights for its frontier open model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), on Hugging Face. Made available for preview just three weeks ago, the French AI company says ML4 has significantly improved since then, thanks to reinforcement learning and testing with customers and partners. Now, it claims, ML4 is the “best open agentic coding model in the world,” beating GLM-5.3 on cybersecurity and coding benchmarks (though only barely on the latter), at a fraction of the cost, Mistral says. “We want to be in a position in which we dictate the frontier.” From here, the AI company promises continued growth. In an embargoed press briefing attended by The New Stack , Pierre Stock , Mistral’s VP of Science, calls ML4 merely “a stepping stone,” saying, “We want to be in a position in which we dictate the frontier.” Mistral’s VP of Science doesn’t want to live in a world without open weights Stock told reporters that Mistral fully supports “the power of open weight,” calling it essential to ensure business continuity, transparency, and auditability for everyone: “I’m not comfortable living in a world in which open weights [don’t] exist,” he said. “I’m not comfortable living in a world in which open weights [don’t] exist,” he said. Recalling when OpenAI announced plans to cut off Cursor’s direct access to its models or when the US government ordered Anthropic to suspend Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all foreign nationals , Stock’s case for open weights bears weight — perhaps why he says the philosophy is in the French company’s DNA. “Our stance is that AI is going to be like electricity.” “Our stance is that AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor or an oligopoly can cut off electricity from one day to another.” Mistral puts open weights at the center of its approach. Anthropic CEO and co-founder Dario Amodei has argued that open weights alone cannot resolve the concentration of AI power because access to computing infrastructure remains concentrated. As Stock points out, this way, “nobody can switch it off because it can run either on your infrastructure or on an infrastructure that you can trust.” Coding + cyber = the biggest impact An open-weight model, though, does need the goods to back it up, and Mistral says ML4 is there, calling it “the best open model built in the West.” To back those claims, the company points to Terminal-Bench 4.0, one component of Artificial Analysis’s Coding Agent Index, where, by Mistral’s numbers, Le Chonk — Mistral’s official nickname for ML4 — ranks as the top open model in the world for agentic coding, scoring 41% to Muse Spark Open’s 6%, Kimi K3’s 21%, and just eking past GLM 5.3’s 40%. Click to enlarge image. ( Source: Mistral ) “What the graph doesn’t tell you,” Stock said, “is that it’s more efficient than the competitors,” adding that Le Chonk uses 47% fewer tokens per task on average than GLM 5.3. “It means that you can get things done way faster and at a lower cost,” he explained. Coding prowess, however, wasn’t the startup’s only focus when training its model. “We identified, really, coding and cyber as the two main areas that impact and that can benefit our customers and help them transform their entire business with AI,” Stock said in the briefing. So Mistral backed investments to advance the model’s cyber capabilities. In CyberGym E2E from the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which tests defensive cybersecurity capabilities, the French model once again pulls ahead of much of the competition, scoring 79% to GLM-5.3’s 29% (though Z.ai’s smaller GLM-5.3 Flash scored 74% in the same…

articles.title: ‘Shaking from head to toe’ — How the facial recognition blame game leaves shoppers stranded
articles.content: Mary could tell that her husband was “distraught” the moment he was wrongly accused of shoplifting and ordered to leave Home Bargains. The ordeal left him feeling “isolated”. “I was scared to go into a shop,” he said. They had only popped out to pick up some vitamins. Elsewhere, a woman’s husband was left “shaking from head to toe” after she was told to leave Budgens on account of stealing “loads of meat” the week before. “My mind was racing,” she said. They hadn’t been to that shop for months. Facial recognition is an inherently personal and intimate technology. It scans your features, processes your biometric data and, depending on its results, can stop you from entering a particular space. It might all take place in an instant but its impact extends far and can be surprisingly long lasting — something that is made all the worse by a dizzying lack of clarity about who is to blame when something goes wrong. ‘Taste the indifference’ Earlier this week, in a cramped room in the House of Commons, people wrongly accused of shoplifting by facial recognition technology met to discuss their experiences with Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent South, Dr Allison Gardner. The event, sponsored by the civil liberties group Big Brother Watch, was designed to give people an opportunity to air their grievances with politicians, the media, and the companies involved. Above all, perhaps, it gave everyone the chance to get some answers about how the system works, who is to blame when it doesn’t work as intended, and to start planning how best to move forward. Big Brother Watch invited Facewatch, the company behind the technology, to attend. It also invited representatives from Sainsbury’s, a company that is currently in the process of introducing facial recognition to 200 of its stores. Neither company sent representatives to the event. On hearing details of one specific case, Dr. Gardner said she “had so many questions.” Was it an algorithm glitch, a shop worker making an honest mistake, or something else? Unfortunately, there was no one to answer the specifics. “You can taste the indifference ,” someone at the back of the room said. “Sainsbury’s is happy to scan its customers’ faces but won’t face the people its technology has harmed,” Jasleen Chaggar, Senior Legal and Policy Officer at Big Brother Watch, later told TechRadar. Each of the testimonies from people wrongly flagged by the technology shared striking similarities. A routine activity was suddenly transformed into a confusing, public ordeal of having to defend themselves against allegations they did not immediately understand. People said they felt “bewildered”, “isolated” and “confused.” However, while the emotional impact was consistent, the specifics of each case were often not. Some people were stopped the moment they walked through the shop doors. Others were confronted at the tills with a full basket. The errors were equally unpredictable. One person was a victim of mistaken identity, while another saw their face flagged on an overhead screen. One woman was wrongly intercepted simply because the system had identified the people walking in directly behind her. There was talk of algorithms, of bias and poorly configured training data, of mechanisms for redress, and off-the-record chats about how some managed to gather more information. The overarching feeling was one of bureaucratic exhaustion. Shoppers were left with no clear path to clear their names. “I didn’t know who to turn to,” one person said. articles.title: US data centers could wipe out 15 years' worth of progress in greenhouse gas emissions, report claims — buildouts could emit as much carbon dioxide as all of Mexico
articles.content: Concerns have been mounting everywhere about the environmental impact of data centers, with alarms ringing at various environmental think tanks. The Sierra Club, one of the oldest environmental preservation organizations in the U.S., has now put forth an estimate that by 2030, U.S. data center buildouts will be outputting as much carbon dioxide as the entirety of Mexico, pushing back progress on greenhouse gas reduction by 15 years, Bloomberg reports. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The Club's principal advisor for climate and energy, Jeremy Fusher, puts it plainly: "the numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds." He's referring to an estimate that with the output from pending data center builds, the output from the U.S. power sector is set to put 2.1 billion metric tons of CO2 in the atmosphere by the end of the decade, an uptick of 42% compared to 2025 figures. The researchers' previous estimates were between a quarter and half of the current projections. An increasing number of countries and states are enacting laws demanding that new data center builds have a large portion of their power generated by green sources. However, those laws rarely apply retroactively, and oftentimes have a phase-in period. Even the Irish law on the matter demanding that new data centers be fed by 80% of renewable power only requires that that happens six years after they're powered up. In the current AI-driven market, speed of construction is king. Roughly 40% of U.S. data centers are fed by natural gas turbines , and the situation doesn't look like it'll be changing much. It'll likely get worse, as the addition of green sources almost assuredly won't keep up with demand. Much like RAM, GPUs, and storage, turbines were all slurped up by data centers. Their prices have risen by 50%, and production is backlogged for years, with one maker stating it's opening slots for production in 2032 . Having said all that, Brendan Pierpont from Energy Innovation, another climate-concerned organization, points out that although the current path looks dangerous for the environment, it's hard to make a hard prediction of how the situation will play out. He justifies his position with common data center roadblocks: the availability of turbines, delays in grid connections, and other delay factors. Truth be told, at this point it's hard to predict how many data centers will actually reach completion, given that requests for permits far exceed available grid capacity across the U.S., and a sizable number of buildouts are encountering strong opposition . Plus, although the AI bubble is still alive and well, concerns started to arise about the economics of hyperscalers, indicating some may go the way of the dodo — and their projects along with them.
articles.author: Bruno Ferreira

articles.title: Apple Releasing HomePod Mini 2 Tomorrow With These New Features
articles.content: Following more than two weeks of pre-orders , the HomePod mini 2 will begin arriving to customers and launch in stores this Friday, October 30. Siri AI will be one of the HomePod mini 2's key upgrades, but the feature will not be available at launch. Apple said Siri AI support on the speaker will arrive in a future software update , but it did not say when the update will be released. Siri AI is the more intelligent and personalized version of Siri powered by Apple Intelligence that launched on the iPhone 15 Pro and newer in September. HomePod mini 2 is powered by the Apple Watch Series 10's S10 chip, up from the Apple Watch Series 5's S5 chip in the original HomePod mini. Apple said the S10 chip enables "advanced computational audio," but it did not explicitly confirm if the HomePod mini 2 has improved sound quality compared to the original model. The speaker now supports faster Wi-Fi 6E, up from Wi-Fi 4. The new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K can connect to four HomePod mini 2 or full-sized HomePod 2 speakers in front and rear pairs, allowing for surround sound. Many home theater enthusiasts will prefer to use a proper 5.1 surround sound system with a center speaker and a subwoofer, but this basic all-Apple system at least exists now, and Apple says the front two HomePods virtualize the center channel to some extent. Note that you mix and match HomePod mini 2 and full-sized HomePod 2 speakers for surround sound, so long as the front and rear pairs match. For example, you could have two full-sized HomePod 2 speakers as the front pair and use two HomePod mini 2 speakers as the rear pair. A related Whole Room Audio feature is offered for parties. You can set the HomePod mini 2 as the default audio output on Macs with Wi-Fi 6E and later . The full-sized HomePod 2 also supports this capability now — make sure to install the latest HomePod software version 27.2 via Apple's Home app. There are three Siri microphones in the HomePod mini 2, down from four in the previous model. With the new Sound Glow feature, the top of the HomePod mini 2 glows and pulses in sync with the music playing. You do not need the new model, though, as a software update extended this feature to the original HomePod mini and the full-sized HomePod 2. HomePod mini 2 is available in all-new green and pink color options, along with blue, midnight, and white. In the U.S., the speaker is priced at $149. The previous model was initially $99, but Apple increased the price to $129 in June . articles.title: Orion's temperature control mattress cover is a dream as nights get colder — shop now and save up to $400
articles.content: Last night as I cuddled deeper into my layers of blankets, I found my mind drifting dreamily to the Orion Sleep System. This smart mattress cover, now with up to $400 off at Orion , uses climate control technology to ensure your bed is snug and warm, even on bitterly chilly nights. I tested the Orion Sleep System earlier this year and I think it's one of the best smart beds you can buy. It's now sitting in our Sleep Lab, ready to undergo thermal cam tests, and I've been missing its clever temperature adaptations. Using a series of sensors, it always knew how warm or cool I wanted to be. Right now there's $350 off a queen Orion Sleep System, which is among the best sales we've seen from the brand. I'll be closely watching for deals in the upcoming Black Friday mattress sales but you're unlikely to save much more than this... Sleep System (queen): was $2395 now $2045 There's currently up to $400 off at Orion, with a $350 saving on a queen size reducing it from $2,395 to $2,045. That's a better sale than usual from Orion and although we're hoping for another big price drop on Black Friday, we can't guarantee it. The upfront price is all you pay with Orion, as no subscriptinis required. But if you want sleep tracking , you can add it for $250/year. Our Orion Sleep System review : ★★★★½ View Deal What is a smart mattress cover? The best cooling mattresses use things like cooling fibers, copper infusions and open springs to draw heat away from your bed. That's not what the Orion does. This smart mattress cover, and others of its ilk, is fitted with a series of water tubes, all attached to a central control system. These pipes cool and warm throughout the night, responding to your temperature to keep you comfy. In summer, that means your bed stays cool even in the heatwaves . I tested it during a September where overnight temperatures were all over the place and the Orion ensured I kept a cool head. (Image credit: Future) But right now, I'm dreaming of warmer climes. And one of the magical things about the Orion is that it can pre-warm your bed. It's like a high-tech hot water bottle, only instead of having to kick it out when I inevitably overheat, the Orion automatically turns the temperature down as needed. And it heats back up again in the morning. Rather than waking up to an icy room, it's like I've been gently roused by the warmth of the sun. There's one thing to note, however. The Orion is a smart mattress cover so it fits onto your existing bed. If you're looking for a new mattress entirely, I recommend starting with our best mattress guide. Or try this instead... Pod 6 (twin): was $1999 now $1899 You'll need to sign up to the mailing list to secure $100 off at Eight Sleep, which should reduce a queen size from $2,899 to $2,799. We are hoping to see a bigger price drop for Black Friday but shop now if you can't stand another chilly night. Eight Sleep offers similar smart cooling and heating to the Orion, as well as an integrated alarm for gentle wake ups. You'll also need to pay for sleep tracking, which starts at $17/month. articles.title: Major US Homeland Security breach exposes details on 41,000 employees — undercover ICE agents and contractors unmasked in ‘Icepick’ data dump
articles.content: DHS data breach exposes personal details of over 41,000 employees and contractors The information includes personal information on ICE agents, as well as details of surveillance operations and tools used by undercover agents Numerous high-level officials across US government agencies have been named within the breach The details of over 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors has surfaced online, including staffers at Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and US Customs and Border Protection, following an apparent data breach. The leak contains sensitive information such as email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses for employees alongside internal information on how Homeland Security conducts undercover operations and surveillance programs. The archive was published by a group calling itself the Department of Peace. They dubbed the leak ‘Icepick’, and shared a note stating, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” ‘Icepick’ data dump exposes agents and contractors The DHS has been locked in a battle with activists, protestors, and anonymous social media users who have been tracking and cataloguing the movements and behavior of ICE employees. In response to protests and activist activity, the DHS has expanded its definition of “doxing” - the malicious exposure of personal information such as home addresses - to include basic information such as names. The Icepick data leak has since been turned into a searchable database by Swiss cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew, who said, “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them.” “The DHS especially as an agency completely lacks accountability, despite many parts of it being incredibly unpopular,” crimew said. “The people who work there know this too; for example, some of their LinkedIn bios simply say ‘stuff at US Government’.” Of the 41,000 records exposed, around 10,000 belong to ICE employees, 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and a further 1,000 are Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency accounts. Details on DHS operations contains references to “Keyhole” - an undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups that took place earlier this year - alongside references to a Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” Tools used by employees have also been revealed in the breach, which include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform, the PenLink platform used to analyze phone records and social media, and AI platforms such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. According to the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, who verified the leak on behalf of Wired , the data was obtained from the DHS's Okta login system. An Okta spokesperson said, “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.” A DHS spokesperson said that the agency is “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available”

articles.title: There’s one week left to preorder the Ocarina of Time remake for $10 off
articles.content: The long-awaited remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 launches next Thursday, November 5th. In other words, you have a week remaining to secure your physical edition with a $10 discount at Amazon and Walmart . Once the game launches, the physical version will almost certainly go from $59.99 to $69.99 while the digital version will stay at $59.99. The Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time (Switch 2) Where to Buy: $69.99 $59.99 at Amazon (preorder, physical) $69.99 $59.88 at Walmart (preorder, physical) Nintendo had the unenviable task of reimagining its Nintendo 64-era masterpiece for the Switch 2, and based on our hands-on time with some sections of the game , it’s a lot of fun to play. The graphics and art style are fantastic, and the controls have been modernized to be simpler to pick up for those who are already experienced with third-person action games, including other modern Zelda titles. window.HYPE_DESK_CONFIG = { productImageUrl: "https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/ipad_mini_6.png", productImageAlt: "iPad mini 6 (2021, A15 series)", productTitle: "iPad mini 6 (2021, A15 series)", shortDescription: "Pick up a refurbished iPad mini for less", longDescription: "The compact 8.3-inch iPad mini features Apple's A15 Bionic chip and is a great option for entertainment, reading, and travel. Shop refurbished models at Back Market.", purchaseUrl: "https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=18275&awinaffid=299513&platform=dl&ued=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.backmarket.com%2Fen-us%2Fp%2Fipad-mini-2021-a15-series%3Futm_source%3Dchatgpt.com", purchaseLinkText: "Shop At Back Market" }; Other great Verge-approved deals It’s tough to find an HDMI dock with more utility than Sharge’s Disk Pro 2 . Being a dock for your USB-C gadgets is just one of its skills. The dock houses up to an M.2 2280-size SSD, letting it serve as external storage for your devices to read from or write to. Additionally, it has some useful ports (beyond its HDMI 2.1 4K/144Hz port), like a 5Gbps USB-A port, SD and microSD card slots, plus USB-C passthrough charging for up to 80W. Plus, it has a built-in magnet to let it snap to your iPhone, so long as it supports MagSafe. The “Ultra” version I’ve described costs $80.91 (originally $109.90) once you clip the on-page coupon for 10 percent off. Check out my colleague Sean’s informative and fun hands-on. Do something a little different with your night or weekend by snagging a Play-Doh Blooms kit . It’s not for everyone, but for those who’ve been tempted to build (or gift) a Lego floral bouquet, these Blooms kits look a lot more realistic. Also, they seem fun to piece together, and each set includes all the tools you need to assemble and preserve the flowers. There are several Blooms models, but the Rosy Petite bouquet kit is $18.74, down from $24.99, at Amazon . If you’re already shopping for the holidays, this seems like a nice stocking stuffer. We highlighted this deal recently, but it’s still happening and worth sharing again. Best Buy is one of the few retailers that still sells the M4-equipped Apple Mac Mini desktop , and it’s the only one that’s currently discounting it. Originally $599 when it debuted in 2024, its price increased due to RAMageddon (plus, it was really hard to find in stock). It’s cheaper now for the 16GB RAM / 256GB SSD configuration than it has been for a while, costing you $649. While the M4 model has been outclassed by the new, moderately faster M6 version that’s $779 at Amazon (originally $899), the form factor and port selection are nearly identical. As in, it’s a mini, yet mighty macOS desktop that’s capable of more than you might expect.

articles.title: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 prices hit $2,000, costing more than the RTX 5090 did at launch and with limited stock available — original $999 MSRP long forgotten, with prices now 2-3x higher
articles.content: The Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080, Nvidia's second-fastest GPU from its current generation, now costs as much as the RTX 5090 did, on paper, when it launched. Prices have reached $2,000 and higher, with most of the available stock online limited to third-party sellers. If you can find it in stock, it may end up costing you two to three times as much as it did when it launched. The cheapest, in-stock RTX 5080 available to buy from a reputable seller online for delivery is this PNY RTX 5080 for $1,999 from Best Buy , the same price as the RTX 5090's on-paper MSRP. You might otherwise end up paying $2,299.99, at least, for this Asus ROG Astral mode at Newegg , or you could pay nearly $3000 for this Gigabyte RTX 5080 from MemoryC, now priced at $2,983.23 . Stock for the RTX 5080 is otherwise limited everywhere, with just one or two available for local pickup (in Best Buy's case), and limited options for delivery. You can also find similar in-store-only pricing at Micro Center, depending on location, which has a Gigabyte card for $1,979.99. You'll also see a lot of the listings online from sketchy, third-party sellers.. For instance, you could pay at least $2,211.17 for this PNY RTX 5080 from a third-party Amazon seller . Empowered PC, the seller for this card, has had 81% positive ratings over the last 12 months, with 202 ratings in total. Reputable seller or not, this price scale means you're paying significantly more than the $999 launch price for this GPU. As our GPU price tracking shows, though, this isn't an isolated case. RTX 5080 prices have, like the rest of the RTX 50-series, risen steadily since it launched. However, this is the first time that its price floor has been around the RTX 5090's launch price. That PNY RTX 5080, for instance, was being sold for around $1,500 on average back in August. It's a bitter pill for gamers, though, that the RTX 5080 has now reached and breached the RTX 5090's launch pricing. That GPU has an MSRP of $1,999, although it'll now cost you thousands more. Prices for the RTX 5090 hit as high as $9,500 last month , but the situation is even worse today. What little stock that remains on sale online can be found for as high as $12,000. The RTX 5080 uses Nvidia's GB203 GPU and comes with 10,752 CUDA cores, along with 16GB of GDDR7 VRAM. Unfortunately, it, like the rest of the consumer gaming GPU market, is being affected by AI. Demand for high-end GPUs hasn't stopped, but Nvidia's attention has shifted to the enterprise market. So, too, has the focus of memory manufacturers, meaning DRAM allocations and production lines that would otherwise produce memory chips for graphics cards have instead gone to feeding the demand for high-margin HBM for AI data centers .

articles.title: HyperX Omen 35L review: A polished gaming PC for deep pockets
articles.content: HP’s HyperX Omen 35L is ambitious, and it’s hard not to be impressed by it in our maxed-out test guise with a Ryzen 9 9950X3D and Nvidia RTX 5080. From its monochrome design and extensive RGB lighting to its top-tier components, it checks the boxes enthusiasts are looking for. But when a PC is $6,211 like our test configuration, it raises the question of whether the Omen 35L’s blend of style, performance, and premium features is enough to justify a purchase, even if that's what high-end PCs cost right now. Design of the HyperX Omen 35L The HyperX Omen 35L’s black and white case stands out, looking refreshingly modern, even though parent company HP has used similar designs before. At 8.27 by 16.06 by 16.14 inches, it’s firmly in mid-tower territory. The metal case feels reassuringly solid and makes extensive use of tempered glass. Bright RGB fans shine through the front while many RGB-lit components are visible through the side panel. It’s a classy system. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The contrast continues inside, where the black motherboard, graphics card, and power supply are easily visible against the white case. The white liquid cooling loops are especially attractive, as is the CPU cooler featuring its own LCD panel. The latter shows CPU and GPU temperatures. HyperX Omen 35L Specifications CPU AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D Motherboard HP AMD B850 Memory 64GB DDR5-6000 (2x 32GB) Graphics Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 (16GB GDDR7, 2,617 MHz boost clock) Storage 2x 1TB PCIe 5.0 SSDs (non-RAID) Networking Realtek 8922AE Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0 Front Ports 10 Gbps USB-C, 2x 5 Gbps USB-A, audio combo jack Rear Ports 2x 10 Gbps USB-C, 2x 5 Gbps USB-A, 4x USB 2.0, DisplayPort 1.4, Ethernet Power Supply 1,000 W fully modular Cooling 240 mm LCD liquid cooler Operating System Windows 11 Pro Dimensions (WxDxH) 8.27 x 16.06 x 16.14 inches (210 x 408 x 410 mm) Price (as configured) $6,210.98 Ports and Upgradeability on the HyperX Omen 35L HyperX’s top-mounted front ports include USB-C (10 Gbps), two USB-A (5 Gbps), and an audio combo jack. This location works well if the desktop is on the floor. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware At the back, the tower offers a pair of USB-C ports (10 Gbps), two USB-A (5 Gbps), four USB 2.0, DisplayPort 1.4 output, Ethernet, and audio jacks. It’s disappointing to see a desktop this expensive offers neither USB4 nor Thunderbolt 4, though it does include Wi-iFi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0 from a Realtek 8922AE networking card. The wireless antennas are built into the chassis, eliminating the need for external protrusions. It’s also notable that HP offers a Clear CMOS button, a surprise on a mainstream tower. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The HyperX Omen 35L offers about as much upgradeability as expected from a mid-tower, without proprietary parts. Its side doors are secured with thumbscrews; the slide rearward and away. The mATX-style motherboard offers four DDR5 DIMM slots, populated in our review unit with two 32GB RGB HyperX modules running at 6,000 MHz. The system also supports two M.2 2280 drives. The primary slot is covered in a substantial heatsink just above the RTX 5080. Accessing the other slot requires removing the RTX 5080. The card is secured with five screws, two of which hold it to the front support bracket. Deft fingers are required to reinstall the screws at the back of the card. HP’s wiring work is tidy for a mainstream tower. Sleeved cables would have improved the refinement. On the plus side, HP includes a fully modular power supply, an uncommon feature in big box systems. Gaming and Graphics on the HyperX Omen 35L We tested the HyperX Omen 35L in a maxed-out configuration featuring a Ryzen 9 9950X3D processor, 64GB of RAM, and a GeForce RTX 5080. I fired up 007 First Light to test out this system’s prowess. At a 3840 x 2160 resolution with high settings and post effects enabled, I saw up to 120 frames per second (fps) indoors and in the mid-90 fps range in more complex scenes without DLSS.…

articles.title: AWS Elastic Beanstalk for regulated workloads: Built for the next decade, not just the first deploy
articles.content: For more than a decade, the managed application platform industry has optimized around a compelling promise: get code running as quickly as possible. Five-minute deployments. Git-based workflows. Minimal configuration. Infrastructure abstracted away from developers. That simplicity changed how software gets built, and for good reason. Application teams should spend more time building software and less time assembling infrastructure. But for organizations in regulated industries, getting an application running is only the beginning. A patient scheduling system, financial application, government service, or aerospace workload may remain in production for years. During that time, operating systems need patching. Runtimes reach end of support. Security requirements evolve. Applications scale. Teams change. Auditors ask for evidence. Regulatory frameworks expand. For these organizations, the question is no longer simply: How quickly can we deploy? It is: How easily can we deploy, and keep that application secure, supported, observable, auditable, and operational for years? “The services built for fast starts also need to support long stays.” That is why platform selection for regulated workloads runs on three axes rather than one. Developer simplicity still matters. But compliance posture and service continuity decide whether that simplicity survives an audit or a roadmap change. The missing middle in regulated industries Large enterprises often address this challenge by building specialized organizations around their applications: platform engineering teams , SRE organizations, cloud centers of excellence, security engineering teams, FinOps practices, and dedicated compliance functions. Many mid-size organizations operate under similar regulatory expectations without comparable specialization. A healthcare software company still needs to satisfy HIPAA requirements. A financial services company still operates within PCI DSS or SOX controls. Government contractors encounter FedRAMP requirements. Data residency, security reviews, vulnerability remediation, access controls, and audit evidence don’t disappear just because an organization has fewer engineers. Regulatory obligations do not scale down with the size of the engineering organization. That creates a difficult operating equation. These teams need production-grade infrastructure and strong governance. But every hour their application developers spend maintaining deployment infrastructure, investigating platform issues, patching underlying systems, or reconciling configuration is an hour not spent improving the applications the business depends on. Workforce shortages in specialized IT roles compound the problem: the team keeping a patient scheduling application running is frequently the same team preparing audit evidence. This is not a question of technical maturity. It is an operating-model problem. The applications already exist Modernization discussions often begin with the destination: containers, cloud-native architectures, microservices, and increasingly sophisticated infrastructure platforms. Regulated organizations rarely have the luxury of beginning with a blank sheet of paper. A mid-size healthcare organization might operate patient portal front-ends on Java and Tomcat, HL7 integration services on .NET and IIS, patient intake workflows in PHP, and lab data pipelines in Python. All in audit scope, all maintained by the same small team that also manages network security and prepares evidence for the next compliance review. Every organization has a modernization roadmap. Most are longer than the compliance calendar is patient. “Every organization has a modernization roadmap. Most are longer than the compliance calendar is patient.” That creates an important test for any application platform intended for this market: Can it improve how organizations operate the applications they have today, not only the applications they hope to build…

articles.title: 4 tips on how to get started with consumer-friendly AI agents
articles.content: Agentic artificial intelligence is gaining popularity far beyond tech circles, with Meta , OpenAI , Anthropic and other companies going head-to-head in the surging market for consumer-friendly AI agents . While the leading AI labs have offered tools with agentic capabilities for years, agents that are designed to work proactively on a user’s behalf for tasks from buying groceries to managing to-do lists have taken off this year. For anyone getting started, it can be overwhelming to understand the differences between the companies’ various offerings and which agents might be best suited for specific tasks. Here are some pointers on where to begin if you’re looking to leverage agents in your personal or professional life — or both. Don’t just use one agent; opt for a ‘stack’ Many people in the tech world turn to multiple agents from different AI labs for both their work and home lives. Why? Because “there’s not one holy grail-like agent right now that could do everything,” said Jose Artigas, a business consultant working on AI strategy. Artigas and many others who use AI agents regularly rely on a “stack” of them, a term that refers to a combination of many tools and technologies. Each company’s consumer-facing agent has a slightly different target function, and they vary in accessibility. Some are free, some require a monthly subscription and others are still in testing modes or otherwise not available to everyone. There are also restrictions on their availability in countries outside of the U.S. Experts say it’s best not to rely solely on one agent if you’re looking to maximize their output and productivity . “What I like to do is to have this system of checks and balances in place where one agent does the work and then I let the other one critique and criticize it, and that way, they find mistakes, correct themselves and become better,” said Clara Gigling, founder of Oudae Labs, a research lab building bespoke tools for agents. Capitalize on each agent’s strengths and weaknesses Each of the major AI companies markets their consumer-facing agents in slightly different ways, often focusing on its ability to help manage either a busy work life or a busy personal life. Anthropic said it built Claude Duet for “professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track.” In contrast, Meta said Muse can help with tasks from “saving money and improving your health to smart shopping and helping you strengthen your relationships.” Claude Duet, OpenAI’s Dots and xAI’s Grok Bot have each been described as aiming to be like a colleague, or even a chief of staff, whereas Muse and Instinct, from the startup Spear Street Technology, have been described as more like personal assistants. But that’s not to say any of them are incapable of helping with tasks outside those realms. Artigas said he’d recommend looking at Claude Duet as key for someone working on a side hustle or launching a new business, Dots as a debugger and problem solver if they’re engaging in any specialized technical work, and Instinct for help with things like sending tedious emails or booking reservations and travel plans. Those are the three consumer-facing agents he uses most often, but Artigas said Muse would be a good place to start for a novice because it’s “very user-friendly,” with many prompts early on to give people ideas of how they can use it. Trial and error is part of the process Your preferences for how you want to interact with an agent, how your agent communicates, and your own assessment of the quality of its work should all factor into which agents you’d like to use — and which tasks you’d like to assign to an agent. Experts recommend testing out agents you’re curious about to help in reaching those determinations. To begin this testing,…

articles.content: Today on Decoder , I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1. Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of anywhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. That would immediately make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet. But the price tag really isn’t the whole story here. The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages filled with details that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab. As you might imagine, that picture is both really complicated and built on a series of very, very ambitious assumptions about the future and what AI will do to it . So I wanted to have Joey on the show to help break down what this document tells us, both about Anthropic’s finances and the broader AI economy. Joey and his colleagues at SemiAnalysis actually built a model of Anthropic’s finances from the outside back in July, so he’s been waiting for this filing about as eagerly as anyone, and I was excited to hear his take on what we’ve learned and, importantly, what we still don’t know. Okay: SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart on the Anthropic S-1 and the costs and risks of building frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Joey Brookhart, you are an analyst at SemiAnalysis. You’re also co-lead on SemiAnalysis’ Tokenomics model, which is going to come up a lot in this episode. Welcome to Decoder . Yeah, thanks so much, Nilay. I am very excited to talk to you. We’re talking just a couple days after the big Anthropic S-1 was filed. It’s our first look inside of the finances of one of the leading frontier models. What’s your take? What’s your read into it? It was an awesome S-1. It’s been a rough three weeks since the investor day. Some people were somewhat disappointed in the September [annualized recurring revenue] numbers, but what we saw here was a company that has efficiently scaled to an amazing level, with a $1 trillion-plus valuation, $70 billion-plus of ARR in a very short amount of time. In gross margins, compute margins, and free cash flow, everything is what you’d want to see. So I don’t think there was much to nitpick in this filing. It’s the reason you’ve seen a lot of the semiconductor complex, and the neoclouds and compute stocks, really rally again in the last two days. It’s funny, I don’t think I can nitpick the S-1 itself. I want to get into some of the details because there are a lot of numbers in there that are worth thinking about. I actually just want to start at the really big picture. You run a thing called Tokenomics. I’m going to explain what Tokenomics is to people. I look at Anthropic and where it could go. I look at Dario Amodei saying that he can see his way to $1 trillion in revenue. Where does that money come from? Because so much of these businesses are about eating every other business and it feels like someone else has to make some money to pay Anthropic to generate these revenues. I haven’t actually seen that laid out very clearly. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? articles.title: FBI leads action to shut down Virtualine bulletproof service linked to major cybercrime activity
articles.content: FBI and international partners seized infrastructure tied to Virtualine, a hosting provider allegedly serving cybercriminals Authorities say the service facilitated phishing, ransomware operations, illicit crypto activity, and other crimes Investigators seized servers and customer data, though no arrests have been announced so far The FBI has announced it seized the website of Virtualine, a bulletproof hosting service that allegedly allowed child pornography, laundered stolen and extorted crypto, and facilitated a wide range of other criminal activities. The operation was carried out in partnership with German and Dutch authorities, as well as multiple private companies, with police raiding a data center in Limburg to seize “dozens of physical servers” that also hosted “hundreds” of virtual servers. As a result, they gained access to information about more than 3,000 of Virtualine’s customers, it was said. “The police are currently taking follow-up actions towards these users,” the Dutch police said, although it’s difficult to say how valuable the information will be, since most bulletproof hosting providers don’t ask for private data, and criminals are good at hiding it, as well. Bulletproof hosting Every website, including hacking forums, criminal service providers, even fraudulent landing pages, needs a server that hosts it. Hosting providers renting out these servers are generally compliant with law enforcement agencies, so when the police requests a takedown or files a complaint, most of them comply. However, there is a subset of hosting providers, colloquially called “bulletproof hosting”, which are unusually resistant to pressure from the authorities. It doesn’t mean all of them are inherently illegal or malicious. There are cases where such services are necessary - in countries with strong censorship, or where website owners want to protect their identities. In this case, however, Virtualine was openly criminal, with the US Department of Justice (DOJ) saying it advertised its services to criminals on cybercrime forums saying, on at least one occasion, “You can use Virtualine for all illegal/black hat activities (including phis[h]ing, carding, email spam, port scanning and all others) except for child contents and terrorism activities.” The company took it a step further. In March 2026, it introduced an “additional protection plan” that offers customers who receive takedown requests “another shell company not affiliated with Virtualine, after which the server is reactivated.” Interestingly enough, Virtualine said it did not accept child porn or terrorism content, but according to the DOJ - did exactly the opposite. One of its clients created a forum that allowed users to post and sell access to “nude, sexually suggestive, and/or sexually explicit images and videos of minors and adults,” while also promoting a hack-for-hire service that broke into people’s accounts and stole their explicit photos and videos. Virtualine was even notified about it by law enforcement agencies from Germany, Canada, and Australia, but decided to ignore the warnings and continue hosting the client. At the same time, Virtualine’s customers were allowed to pay in Bitcoin, offering an unhosted bitcoin address that allowed customers “to direct pay without concern their funds would be flagged as illicit”. Citing Chainalysis data, BleepingComputer said the company’s wallet was seen receiving funds from ransomware operations, infostealers, Russian-language cybercrime forums, and more. “Virtualine then laundered those proceeds to conceal their origin,” the blockchain company added. Piercing the kevlar Besides confiscating the servers and the data, the main website - virtualine.net - was defaced and now shows the usual FBI “this website has been seized” message. Unfortunately, no arrests have been made, which means the service will most likely continue operating. According to BleepingComputer , it is “partially online” but its network prefixes…

articles.title: Systemd adds support for Rust
articles.content: Everyone's favorite Unix init system is adding support for the Unix world's favorite new programming language. What's the worst that could happen? Don't worry, this isn't here just yet. Agent P and his trusty team released systemd version 262 about a month ago. That means that systemd 263 is now under construction, and developer Christian Brauner announced on Mastodon that his new feature has been merged. The previous effort, which was pull request #44144, has now been split into five separate parts. Part 1 contains keyring-util and voa-util , described as "helpers for enrolling certificates into kernel keyrings." Part 2, support programs written in Rust , is the banner item. Then come a few more: bind only the headers Rust code uses , wrap the libsystemd-shared helpers systemd-keyring-setup needs , and finally, add systemd-keyring-setup . There are several important riders to the announcement, and these are spelled out in the second PR: "Rust is only used for new leaf components. Existing C code isn't ported and nothing that other components depend on is written in Rust." In other words, before anyone gets too excited, this does not indicate the start of an effort to rewrite systemd in Rust. All it means is that new systemd modules can be written in Rust. The second bullet point will be more significant for existing Rust developers: "No cargo. Everything is built with meson." Cargo is the Rust language’s package manager and build system. It's the normal way to build Rust applications, as well as to distribute modules of Rust code for other Rust developers to use. However, systemd already has a modern build system. It's called Meson and it's not unique to systemd – it is also used extensively by the GNOME project and the Mesa 3D graphics library. Meson itself is written in Python and uses Ninja to manage the compilation process. Ninja was designed to build Chrome faster , and it's also used for Android . The third stipulation is that any Rust code must not use the standard library . For those more familiar with C, this may sound extreme, but it's normal for embedded Rust programming . The project documents the system requirements. It needs Rust version 1.85 or later. That's modest: that version was released in February 2025 , and version 1.99.1 appeared earlier this month. It also calls for bindgen version 0.71.1 ( from December 2024 ) or newer, and Meson 1.4.0 ( from March 2024 ). These are relatively old versions – for instance, it's the Meson version included in Debian 13). Brauner added an interesting little coda in a second Masto post : saying that the team would have liked to support Rust in the core of systemd, but currently, Rust’s support for dynamic libraries isn't quite there yet. It's perhaps worth noting that writing systemd modules in Rust isn't the same thing at all as calling systemd from Rust code. There are several tools for doing that, and they have been around for years: for example, the systemd crate first appeared in 2015. ®

articles.title: The next Hitman elusive target has Agent 47 taking down a podcaster who is 'loud, paranoid, and completely obsessed with content' — and played by a real-life influencer
articles.content: The next Hitman Elusive Target has been revealed The limited-time mission will see Agent 47 taking down an annoying podcaster The target will be played by real-world content creator Seán McLoughlin The next Hitman Elusive Target has been revealed, and it's something that could happen in 2026. As of October 29, players will be able to take out Finn Colton – a controversial millionaire content creator who goes by the online handle 'Finnvictus'. The mission will see the flashy mansion of the existing Hawke's Bay map turned into an even more elaborate space for content creation, with its own underground studio and cameras that live-stream everything 24/7. Bald assassin protagonist Agent 47 has managed to gain entry thanks to an invite to appear on the content creator's flagship podcast and will have to contend with an environment that has eyes almost everywhere. (Image credit: IO Interactive) That's not all, however, as Colton is played by Seán McLoughlin, better known as 'Jacksepticeye', with the popular streamer lending both his likeness and voice to the character. "I’ve been playing Hitman with my community for years, so getting to actually step into the World of Assassination is unreal," shared McLoughlin. "Finn is loud, paranoid, and completely obsessed with content, and playing him was an absolute blast. I can’t wait to see all the creative ways you take him down." The mission will be available for free for a limited time, though die-hard Hitman fans can pick up a themed DLC pack as well. It costs $7.99 / £6.99 and includes permanent access to the mission via the Elusive Target Arcade mode plus a new suit and some unique equipment to try. Hitman: World of Assassination is available now for PlayStation 5 , PlayStation 4 , Xbox Series X and Series S , Xbox One , and PC, or as Hitman World of Assassination – Signature Edition for Nintendo Switch 2 .

articles.title: Up to 350,000 Macs exposed by a forgotten Popcorn Time updater
articles.content: An abandoned Popcorn Time updater left up to 350,000 Macs vulnerable to remote takeover, giving potential attackers a way to execute malicious code with full system privileges. Popcorn Time Security researchers at Eye Research detailed the discovery in an October 22, 2026, research report about Operation IXIM. The vulnerability affected Time4Popcorn, an abandoned fork of the popular BitTorrent streaming application that continued circulating under the Popcorn Time name after the original project shut down in 2014. Some users had stopped using Popcorn Time, but its updater kept running. Eye Research discovered attackers could hijack it to install malware and intervened between November 2025 and March 2026. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums
articles.author: Andrew Orr <andreworr@appleinsider.com>

articles.title: Ofcom explains how it wants social media platforms to keep out under-16s
articles.content: Ofcom has assessed the best ways of enforcing age checks online The regulator also identifies methods that aren't effective Around 4 in 10 under-16s plan to try to get around the ban in the UK Back in June, the UK government ruled that under-16s should be banned from social media platforms, with enforcement scheduled to start during the first half of 2027. Now the communications regulator Ofcom has set out the ways it expects tech companies to abide by the law. The challenge isn’t simply checking someone’s age. It’s doing so without turning everyday internet use into an identity check. Pieter Arntz, Malwarebytes In its new announcement (via the BBC ), Ofcom highlights four "highly effective" methods for keeping under-16s out of apps and off sites they shouldn't be accessing — and they're all going to be familiar to anyone who's used age-gated services online in recent times. The four methods are photo ID matching (using something like a passport or driving license), bank-based checks (Ofcom says 90% of UK 16-17 year-olds have a bank account), digital ID services (a third-party service like EasyID or Yoti), and facial age estimation via a webcam (which Ofcom says is best deployed as a secondary check). This is a "rapid assessment" from Ofcom, and none of these approaches are confirmed yet — UK lawmakers will take the suggestions on board, and decide the best way to enforce the rules at a later date, most probably before the end of the year. All of these methods can be delivered "in a way that protects users' privacy" according to Ofcom. Ultimately though, it will be down to tech companies to decide how to implement age checks that fulfil the requirements set down by the government. "Here are things that can work, they must preserve privacy, they must protect people's data, but it's on you to put in place what you think works for you," Ofcom CEO Dame Melanie Dawes told the BBC . Challenges ahead The recommendations put forward by Ofcom (Image credit: Ofcom) Ofcom also lists checks that it thinks are ineffective: self-declaration, general contractual agreements, and verifiable parental consent. The regulator also acknowledges that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated", but says that correctly implemented safeguards should "significantly reduce the likelihood" of unauthorized access. In its rapid assessment announcement, Ofcom also encourages app stores to take more responsibility over age checks. Right now, self-declarations are most commonly used to unlock downloads for age-restricted content. The challenge for social media platforms is that teenagers don’t like to be told ‘no’. Olli Krebs, SVP EMEA at Incode These are going to be tough rules to enforce, whatever the approach is: recent research from EE suggests that 42% of 11-15 year-olds are planning to try and get around whatever restrictions are put in place. This could be by switching to apps or platforms not covered by the new laws, including messaging services and gaming sites. Last week Ofcom also admitted that the Online Safety Act introduced in July 2025 had so far made "no significant change" to the harmful content children had been exposed to online. The act was intended to ensure protection from content involving pornography, serious violence, suicide material, racism, misogyny, and bullying. "This finding is concerning and shows that further progress is needed to protect children online," says Ofcom . The regulator also recommended adding material around body stigma and depression to the primary content categories that children should be protected from online. Analysis: What do privacy experts think? (Image credit: natureaddict / Pixabay) Ofcom's proposals are likely to spark some familiar privacy concerns — and security experts told us they aren't without foundation. “The challenge isn’t simply checking someone’s age. It’s doing so without turning everyday internet use into an identity check," said Pieter Arntz, Senior Malware Intelligence…
